In stoppage time Scott McTominay found Neves, who tucked the equaliser into the bottom corner. The match ended after the restart.
The champions deserved credit for creating chances and fighting back, but finishing must improve. Sassuolo are next.
comments: Two posts and a late equaliser. My heart cannot take this.
João hit the post, then rescued us. What a player.
Scott still delivers when it matters.
3.1 xG means chances were there. Improve the finishing.
Two points dropped. Not good enough.
We nearly beat the champions. Proud of Parma.

articles.headline: CHANCES CREATED, POINTS LOST: NAPOLI FINISHING UNDER SCRUTINY
articles.label: PARMA 1–1 NAPOLI
articles.dek: Napoli create 3.1 xG and score only once.
body: Eleven shots, six on target, two strikes against the post and 3.1 xG produced only one Napoli goal at Parma.
Pio and Neves hit the woodwork before Neves equalised late from McTominay’s pass.
The right response is better composure and finishing, not a wholesale tactical overhaul. One game is not a crisis.
comments: Fix the finishing, not the whole attack.
Two posts. I need a holiday.

articles.headline: DAVIES AT 118': NAPOLI BREAK CELTIC HEARTS TO LIFT UEFA SUPER CUP
articles.label: UEFA SUPER CUP · EXTRA-TIME DRAMA
articles.dek: A goalless 90 minutes, an agonising extra time and one decisive switch: Alphonso Davies finishes Pio Esposito's through ball to secure a 1–0 win.
body: Napoli are UEFA Super Cup winners after Alphonso Davies struck in the 118th minute of extra time to defeat Celtic 1–0. For almost two hours the European champions pushed for a breakthrough, but the match remained goalless until the very end.

The first half ended 0–0 despite Napoli holding a 1.2–0.0 advantage in expected goals. The scoreline stayed unchanged through full time. Napoli's control was real, but so was Celtic's resilience, and a trophy that had seemed within reach threatened to drift towards penalties.

Kevin De Bruyne had a late opportunity in the first period of extra time, but the score was still 0–0 after 105 minutes. With time running out, manager Stefan Saladino had already made a tactical intervention designed to exploit Celtic's problems dealing with pace: Michael Olise came off, Lutsharel Geertruida was introduced at full-back and Davies was pushed further forward.

The winner vindicated the move. Pio Esposito threaded a through ball into Davies' path. The Canadian accelerated past his defender, cut back inside the penalty area and shot from just inside the box. The Celtic goalkeeper got a touch, but not enough to keep the ball out. Davies, 118 minutes. Napoli, 1–0.

It was another decisive contribution from Esposito, whose pass turned the manager's late gamble into a trophy-winning moment. It also provided a reminder that a deep, flexible squad is not merely about covering injuries: one positional change can transform a final.

Napoli had started with Meret behind Davies, Buongiorno, captain Bastoni and Kayode; Zaïre-Emery and João Neves in midfield; Paz and Olise supplying Pio and Beier. The manager described the selection as full strength. De Bruyne and Moore also featured in the match, though their precise entry times have not been confirmed.

After back-to-back Serie A titles and a Champions League triumph over Real Madrid, Napoli add another European honour. The story of this Super Cup will be told through one moment: a 105th-minute tactical adjustment, a Pio through ball and a Davies finish in the 118th.
comments: 118 MINUTES AND ALPHONSO DOES THAT. I have no voice left.
The goalkeeper touched it and I stopped breathing until it crossed the line.
Olise off, Geertruida into the back line, Davies higher. This is what in-game management actually looks like.
And we kept a proper defensive shape while chasing the winner.
THROUGH BALL FROM PIO. People will talk about the finish, but that pass is ridiculous.
Pio and Beier are still our foundation. Even on a quiet scoring night, Pio decides it.
One goal in 118 minutes against Celtic and people want a statue? We should have won in normal time.
We won the trophy. Please consider experiencing joy once.
At 117 I had already mentally lost the penalty shootout. Sorry to everyone in my building.
I was negotiating with the universe. Davies did the rest.
Another clean sheet in a final. The captain's defence deserves its flowers.
Meret starts, Napoli shut them out. Important too.
Warren and João starting together in a European final. That's the future right there.
Good platform. We still need more match data before judging the partnership.
Heartbreaking. We held the European champions until minute 118. Respect to our boys.
You made us work for every inch. Respect back.
I would have loved Scott in a battle like that. But the manager got the big call right.
This season the competition for midfield minutes will be brutal.
We dominated the first half on chances and somehow needed extra time. Finals are never simple.
My heart requests a 3–0 next time.
Meret in goal today, Peacock waiting in the wings. Keepers deserve love too.
From full-back to match-winner. 118TH MINUTE. WHAT A PLAYER.
Put the tactical switch in the museum.
All that money and they needed a late winner against Celtic.
Another trophy, another Juventus account watching us celebrate.
Olise going off was tactical, not an indictment of him. Squad football means sacrifices.
Exactly. You can be world-class and still be the right substitution.
Kevin almost had his moment before Davies. Football is cruel and beautiful.
Back-to-back Scudetti. Champions League. Super Cup. I don't want to wake up.
Celtic couldn't live with Mikey's pace. Then we pushed Davies up. They were in trouble.
Two different kinds of nightmare for tired defenders.
A trophy is a trophy. I hate admitting it, but that is a brilliant late winner.

articles.headline: THE SWITCH THAT WON IT: HOW SALADINO UNLEASHED DAVIES AGAINST CELTIC
articles.label: TACTICAL BREAKDOWN · SUPER CUP
articles.dek: With Celtic still holding firm after 105 minutes, Napoli's manager moved Alphonso Davies forward. Thirteen minutes later, the trophy was decided.
body: The scoreline was still 0–0 when Napoli made their defining tactical adjustment against Celtic. The European champions had created the better opportunities but had not found a way through, and extra time was slipping away.

Celtic had struggled to contain Mikey Moore's pace. Rather than simply asking the same attackers to try again, Stefan Saladino changed the distribution of speed across the pitch: Michael Olise was withdrawn, Lutsharel Geertruida was brought in at full-back and Alphonso Davies advanced into a more attacking position.

The decision was not just an offensive gamble. Introducing a recognised defender behind the attacking line allowed Davies to operate higher without leaving the same space exposed in the back four. Exactly how the wide roles were distributed has not been confirmed, but the intention was clear: force a tired defence to cope with another explosive runner.

The winning move came in the 118th minute. Pio Esposito spotted Davies' run and delivered a through ball. Davies outran his defender, cut inside and struck from just inside the area. A touch from the goalkeeper could not prevent the goal.

It would be simplistic to credit a substitution alone. Esposito's timing and vision, Davies' pace and composure, and Napoli's ability to keep the contest level until the decisive moment all mattered. But the tactical intervention created the conditions for the breakthrough.

For a club building multiple rotation plans, the lesson is obvious: versatility has tangible value. Davies can change the game from different areas of the pitch; Geertruida's defensive coverage helps make that possible. Napoli did not need a second starting eleven to win this final. They needed one timely adjustment.
comments: The key isn't just Davies going forward. It's Geertruida allowing it without chaos behind him.
Alphonso at full sprint against tired legs is borderline unfair.
Don't erase the assist in the tactical analysis. Pio sees the run and makes the pass.
Absolutely. The idea creates space; the players still have to execute.
Or maybe score one of the chances in the first 90 and save us the drama?
We could win 8–0 and you'd complain about the ninth.
Moore stretched them first. Davies finished them. That is squad management.
A superstar coming off doesn't make him a problem. This is why flexibility matters.
The midfield had to hold its discipline while we chased it. Unsung work.
The best managers see what the match needs, not just what the team sheet says.
One tactical switch and Naples is acting like it invented football.
No, just won another European trophy.
A 118th-minute winner is why we watch this sport. Never forget that feeling.

articles.headline: NAPOLI LAND ZAÏRE-EMERY: $172.5M DEAL REWRITES THE MIDFIELD FUTURE
articles.label: OFFICIAL · SUMMER 2029
articles.dek: The European champions complete a $172.5 million move for 23-year-old Warren Zaïre-Emery, an 89-rated midfield force whose versatility could reshape Napoli's options.
body: Napoli have completed the signing of Warren Zaïre-Emery for $172.5 million, adding another young elite midfielder to a squad already crowned champions of Italy and Europe. At 23 and rated 89, the new arrival represents an extraordinary statement of intent from the club that lifted the Champions League trophy in Lisbon.

The agreement is substantial in every respect: a five-year contract, crucial squad status, a weekly wage of $225,000 and a $2.5 million signing bonus. There is no release clause. The size of the fee invites scrutiny, but Napoli have invested in more than a single-season solution.

Zaïre-Emery can operate at central midfield, defensive midfield, attacking midfield and right-back. That range gives the champions multiple ways to manage a demanding calendar, though the question of where he plays most often remains an open football debate rather than a settled selection decision.

The most tantalising prospect is a long-term midfield partnership with João Neves, 24 and rated 94. Neves remains in Naples after the club rejected Real Madrid's $318.2 million bid. Together, the pair could form the core of Napoli's midfield for years. Nico Paz offers creativity further forward, while Scott McTominay, Kevin De Bruyne and Anton Stach ensure experience has not disappeared overnight.

Not everyone will celebrate the price without hesitation. A $172.5 million investment carries expectation, and a crucial role in a title-winning squad creates real competition for minutes. Supporters will debate what it means for McTominay and Paz, and whether Zaïre-Emery's flexibility should ever be used to cover for Michael Kayode at right-back.

The move follows Marc Cucurella's $170 million departure to Newcastle United, but it is not a like-for-like replacement. Napoli still have Alphonso Davies and Riccardo Calafiori as left-sided defensive options. This is a decision to strengthen the heart of the team rather than chase a direct replacement.

The transfer market has delivered another reminder of Napoli's changed status. Once a club forced to defend its stars from wealthier suitors, the European champions have now committed a nine-figure sum to one of the continent's most coveted young midfielders. The real verdict will arrive on the pitch. For now, the city has a new name to sing: Warren Zaïre-Emery.
comments: CENTOSETTANTADUE MILIONI. And I am smiling. This club has completely changed.
Two Scudetti and Europe conquered. We are buying for the next five years now.
The fee is enormous, but CM/CDM/RB/CAM versatility is not a gimmick. It changes how many specialists you need on the bench.
Just don't start pretending our actual right-back is expendable.
Exactly. Versatility is insurance, not a reason to bench Kayode.
A hundred and seventy-two million for a player who doesn't even know which position he plays. Sack him.
You said sack him after winning the Champions League too.
And I remain committed to consistency.
This is either a dynasty or the most expensive midfield traffic jam in history.
Both can be true and I'm here for it.
Twenty-three years old, 89 rated, five-year deal. The years matter as much as the money.
Everyone is drawing Neves and Warren together. Scott hasn't vanished, ragazzi.
Competition for minutes is a good problem. Nobody said Scott was finished.
I love this signing but I do NOT want Nico Paz turned into a spectator.
Different roles, different matches. A crowded squad is the challenge now.
Napoli spending like a sovereign wealth fund and pretending it's romantic.
You tried to buy Pio for $331.8m. Sit this one out.
Juve can't buy Pio and now Napoli sign Warren. What a week.
The forwards are going to enjoy having another midfielder who can get the ball to them.
Love the talent. Still want a proper plan for the left side after Cucurella.
From Paris to Naples. You paid a premium, but this is a serious footballer.
We'll take good care of him.
I spent years worrying we'd lose our best players. Now I'm worrying about where to fit the new ones. Progress?
RB coverage is fantastic. Kayode remains my guy.
$172.5m and a crucial role. The pressure on him will be immediate.
Fair. The price tag won't play the matches for him.
Neves 94 and Warren 89. I need the season to start yesterday.
Sell the entire midfield and build a new one around Warren.
This is why nobody lets you near the contract office.
No release clause is the part I'm happiest about. Five years of control.

articles.headline: GRAZIE, MARC: CUCURELLA LEAVES NAPOLI FOR NEWCASTLE IN $170M DEAL
articles.label: FAREWELL TO A CHAMPION
articles.dek: A $118 million bid was rejected. Newcastle returned with $170 million. The club accepted, and Marc Cucurella chose the next chapter. Naples says goodbye to one of its champions.
body: There is a peculiar cruelty to football's summer window. Only weeks after a city celebrates its greatest triumphs, a name that helped make those nights possible can disappear from the team sheet. Marc Cucurella is leaving Napoli for Newcastle United after agreeing personal terms, completing a transfer worth $170 million. He leaves not as an unwanted player, but as a champion who was given a choice — and chose a new challenge.

The numbers are staggering. Newcastle first approached Napoli with an offer of $118 million, already $25 million above the left-back's $93 million market valuation. Stefan Saladino refused. Newcastle came back with $170 million, an increase of $52 million and a fee roughly 83 percent above that valuation. Napoli accepted the revised bid, but the final decision was always Cucurella's. He has now agreed terms with the English club.

This is where the story becomes more than an exercise in transfer arithmetic. Napoli did not have to sell. Their manager had already refused to entertain the idea of dismantling his midfield when Real Madrid arrived with an astonishing $318.2 million offer for João Neves. That bid was rejected outright. Cucurella's case was different: a huge offer, genuine depth at left-back and, crucially, the player's freedom to decide his own future.

Cucurella departs with two Serie A titles and a Champions League winner's medal. Those honours do not tell every story of his contribution. He brought aggression, personality and the sort of relentless commitment that turns a collection of talented players into a dressing room willing to fight for each other. There were more glamorous names on the teamsheet, but trophies are not won by glamour alone.

There is no need to manufacture a feud between player and club. The manager did not want to force him out, and the club made that position clear. Newcastle were permitted to negotiate; Cucurella chose to accept their terms. In an era when every major transfer is framed as betrayal or exile, the truth can be simpler and more dignified: a successful chapter ended on the player's terms.

Napoli will have decisions to make. Alphonso Davies, 28 and rated 90, and Riccardo Calafiori, 27 and rated 87, offer outstanding options on the left, though replacing Cucurella's presence in the dressing room is not a matter of moving names around a tactics board. The fee is enormous, but so is the standard the outgoing defender helped establish.

The club's new season begins with ambition intact. João Neves remains a Napoli player despite Madrid's interest; the champions of Europe have not opened a general auction. Cucurella's transfer is an exceptional decision, not a surrender of the project. He leaves a club that expects to win again, and one that can acknowledge how much he helped it learn to win in the first place.

For Cucurella, there will be a new shirt and a new crowd. For Naples, there will be memories of the relentless left-back who wore blue while this team climbed to the summit of Italy and Europe. No invented final speech is necessary. The medals, the performances and the respect on both sides say enough.
Grazie, Marc. Due Scudetti. Una Champions League. Per sempre uno di noi.
comments: I know $170m is ridiculous money but I still hate seeing Cucu go. He fought for this shirt. GRAZIE MARC 💙
That's the part the spreadsheets can't measure. A champion leaves and it hurts.
We'll look after him. What a player you've sent us.
So the manager who says nobody is bigger than the badge sells a Champions League winner the first time the number gets big enough. Interesting.
He REJECTED 118m and let Marc choose at 170m. And he told Madrid to get lost over João. Read the article.
I read it. I'll judge the replacement when I see one.
Rejecting $318.2m for Neves is some statement. But everyone has a price eventually, don't they?
Apparently not João. Go find another midfielder.
Napoli fans celebrating a defender leaving because the fee is big. Funny how quickly loyalty becomes an accounting exercise.
Nobody is celebrating him leaving. We are thanking him. There is a difference.
$170 million is massive pressure. But the way Napoli fans talk about him makes me excited to see him in black and white.
He will give you everything. Just don't expect him to stop running.
Two league titles and the Champions League. You can't buy those memories back with $170m. Grazie Marc.
That fee for a 30-year-old left-back is outrageous. Newcastle have lost the plot.
Then don't bid for our champions.
I'm glad they didn't pretend he was pushed out. He chose his next chapter. We can be sad and still wish him well.

articles.headline: THE NIGHT NAPLES TOOK EUROPE: BEIER, PIO AND PEACOCK BRING DOWN REAL MADRID
articles.label: THE FINAL · LISBON
articles.dek: A manager who refused Madrid. A striker who refused to be defined by one miss. A young keeper who refused to concede. Napoli 2–0 Real Madrid: European champions.
body: FULL TIME, LISBON — The scoreboard says Napoli 2, Real Madrid 0. It cannot tell you how long Naples has waited for a night that feels like this, or how many times a football club is told that ambition has a ceiling. Tonight, Stefan Saladino's Napoli have lifted the Champions League. The club that was supposed to be the destination for great managers has instead become the opponent defeated by one who chose to stay.

Six minutes. That was all Maximilian Beier needed to give this final its first great jolt. Pio Esposito supplied him, Beier finished, and a match weighted with Madrid's European history suddenly belonged to the team in blue. Before kickoff Saladino had predicted 'fireworks'. He did not have to wait long for the first one.

But this was no gentle coronation. Madrid had more chances in the first half. Peacock, starting with Alex Meret injured, was required four times before the interval. Each save kept the margin at one; each save bought Napoli's attacking talent another chance to make the lead count. For a young goalkeeper carrying the burden of a Champions League final, that is an extraordinary demand.

At half-time the temptation must have been to imagine protecting the narrowest of leads for another 45 minutes. The football that followed offered a better answer: Napoli did not forget how to attack. In the 67th minute Michael Olise was involved in the buildup, Beier turned provider, and Pio Esposito put the ball in the net. The same two men who had combined for the first goal combined for the second, only with their roles reversed.

Two goals up did not mean the work was finished. At 75 minutes Peacock pushed a Madrid attempt just wide of the post, another intervention on a night of at least five confirmed saves. At 81 minutes Pio threatened a third from a tight angle, but Thibaut Courtois stopped him. One goalkeeper preserved Madrid's faint hope; the other protected Napoli's European crown.

And then the whistle. No comeback, no qualification, no more arithmetic. Napoli had beaten Real Madrid in the Champions League final, 2–0. Beier and Pio had a goal and an assist each. Peacock had his clean sheet. The season had its defining result.

The history behind it makes the moment larger. Napoli have won back-to-back Serie A championships, completing the 2028–29 league campaign with 93 points, 28 wins, nine draws and a single defeat. They also know what heartbreak feels like: Milan beat them in the Coppa Italia final on penalties after a 2–2 draw. That loss does not vanish. It makes the European victory feel earned rather than inevitable.

Last summer Real Madrid approached Saladino about becoming their manager. He declined. Before this final he explained that he felt Napoli were 'BUILDING something special' and that he needed to see it through. He also rejected the suggestion that beating Madrid would somehow prove his choice correct. The decision was about commitment, not a single opponent.

Saladino told supporters before the final that his players put the crest on the front of the shirt before the name on the back. That is the sentence this final will be remembered alongside. Not because it guaranteed a trophy — he explicitly said results could not be guaranteed — but because the players made the commitment visible in the biggest match of their season.

The Coppa Italia trophy went elsewhere. The league title stayed in Naples. And now the European Cup belongs to Napoli. A project has become a champion; an ambition has become a question for every opponent in Europe. How do you stop a team that believes it is still building?

articles.headline: THE PENALTY MISS, THE PROMISE, THE PERFECT EXCHANGE: PIO AND BEIER OWN LISBON
articles.label: THE PARTNERSHIP
articles.dek: One assisted the other. Then the roles reversed. Behind two goals lies a season of trust, scrutiny and two strikers learning to create.
body: Two names, two goals, two assists between them, and a Champions League trophy. On the scoresheet the arithmetic is almost absurdly neat: Beier scored from Pio Esposito's pass in the sixth minute; Pio scored from Beier's in the 67th. Football partnerships are rarely this symmetrical on the night that matters most.

The first goal established the pattern: Pio was not simply waiting for service, and Beier was not simply there to create it. Napoli's forwards were prepared to switch roles without losing the instinct to attack the goal. It is the kind of relationship that cannot be reduced to a pair of individual goal totals.

The second goal told the story again, this time with Michael Olise involved in the buildup. Olise to Beier, Beier to Pio, and Napoli were 2–0 ahead against Real Madrid. At 81 minutes Pio almost added another from a difficult angle, only for Courtois to intervene. Even with the trophy within sight, the striker was still searching for the next opening.

That matters particularly for Pio. In the Coppa Italia final against Milan, he had scored Napoli's 90th-minute equalizer to force extra time and eventually penalties. He then missed his attempt in the shootout Milan won. Football's most unforgiving shorthand could have reduced his contribution to that one kick.

Saladino refused to let it. In the pre-final press conference, he reminded reporters that without Pio's equalizer there would have been no shootout. He pointed to the 85th-minute winner against Juventus in the Champions League semifinal. 'One missed penalty means nothing,' he said. The manager did not promise that Pio would score in Lisbon; he simply refused to let one failure erase an entire season.

Beier's contribution is just as important. He scored early to put Madrid under pressure, then had the composure and awareness to make the pass that allowed Pio to double the lead. The German's willingness to create, rather than force a second goal for himself, is the essence of why this partnership works.

Saladino admitted before the final that he had brought in enough playmaking quality through midfield and out wide to accommodate two goal-oriented strikers. What surprised him was their development as playmakers themselves. Lisbon provided the clearest illustration possible.

There is an easy temptation to call Pio's goal redemption and move on. That is too small a story. The larger one is that Napoli never stopped trusting him, Beier never stopped combining with him, and neither forward needed to be the lone hero. On the night Napoli became champions of Europe, they made each other better.

articles.headline: FOUR SAVES BEFORE THE BREAK. ONE MORE AT 75. PEACOCK'S IMPOSSIBLE NIGHT
articles.label: THE GOALKEEPER
articles.dek: Meret was unavailable. Real Madrid had the chances. A 74-rated youngster made himself indispensable to a European final.
body: Every Champions League final produces images that become shorthand for the night. Napoli will remember Beier scoring early and Pio finishing the second. But ask what made those moments count, and the answer leads to the young goalkeeper at the other end.

Peacock was not supposed to be the obvious headline. Alex Meret was injured and unavailable for the final. Napoli had to trust a young replacement rated 74 in their squad assessments, against a Real Madrid side whose European reputation needs no introduction.

The first half was an examination, not a procession. Madrid created more chances, and Peacock made four saves before the break. Napoli led 1–0 because Beier had finished his opportunity; they still led 1–0 because their goalkeeper had answered Madrid's.

Goalkeeping is a brutal profession in this particular kind of match. A striker can miss and find another opening. A goalkeeper can do everything correctly for 70 minutes and still be remembered for one mistake. Peacock was asked to maintain his concentration with the trophy at stake, against an opponent that kept looking for a way back.

At 67 minutes Pio gave him a second goal of protection. Eight minutes later, Madrid threatened again. Peacock pushed the effort narrowly past the post at 75 minutes. It was the kind of save that turns a seemingly comfortable scoreline into a reminder of how quickly a final can change.

The confirmed match events give him at least five saves and a clean sheet. There is no need to embellish the count or manufacture acrobatics that were never reported. Four saves in the first half against Madrid, another vital intervention late, and no goals conceded in a Champions League final: those facts are dramatic enough.

Peacock's night also says something about the squad Saladino has built. Before the final, the manager specifically named young players including Pio, Mikey Moore and Peacock when explaining why he had stayed in Naples. He wanted to develop them, not use their progress as a stepping stone elsewhere.

The goalkeeper did not win this trophy alone. Beier and Pio supplied the goals, and Napoli protected the lead as a team. But the clean sheet is his, and the importance of his saves cannot be separated from the result. On the biggest stage available, Peacock gave Napoli exactly what they needed.

Some players announce themselves with a spectacular goal. Peacock's announcement came through a refusal to let Madrid score. When Napoli look back on Lisbon, his name will belong in the first sentence, not the footnotes.

articles.headline: MADRID OFFERED HIM THEIR BENCH. SALADINO BUILT A THRONE IN NAPLES INSTEAD.
articles.label: THE SALADINO ERA
articles.dek: This is not a revenge story. It is a story about staying, developing a squad and refusing to confuse prestige with purpose.
body: Imagine the pitch last summer. Real Madrid, one of the most decorated clubs in football, approached Stefan Saladino. For many managers the decision would scarcely have required a second conversation. The prestige, the expectation, the history: Madrid have spent generations representing the summit of the game.

Saladino said no. Not because he dismissed Madrid's history — he repeatedly praised it — but because he believed there was unfinished work in Naples. He had a squad to develop, an identity to deepen, and an ambition that could not be outsourced to another club's trophy cabinet.

That decision became a fixation for the Spanish press before the Champions League final. Was staying safe? Would beating Madrid validate the rejection? Had he made the wrong career move? Saladino grew visibly impatient with the repeated premise. His response was consistent: this was not personal, and a single result would not determine the value of his decision.

'My story is one intertwined with Napoli for the moment,' he told MARCA. To another reporter he named Pio Esposito, Mikey Moore and Peacock as examples of young players he had brought in to develop. He was not interested in turning them into a platform from which to leap toward a supposedly greater club.

Now comes the cinematic irony. In Lisbon, Napoli beat Real Madrid 2–0 to become champions of Europe. Pio supplied Beier for the first goal and scored the second from Beier's assist. Peacock, one of the young players Saladino had mentioned by name, kept a clean sheet in Meret's absence.

It is tempting to declare the decision vindicated. But doing so would ignore what Saladino actually said. His commitment was never contingent on beating Madrid. That is precisely what makes the result so powerful: the trophy follows the principle rather than creating it.

The wider record is staggering. Napoli have won consecutive Serie A titles, with 93 points in 2028–29, and now the Champions League. The Coppa Italia final defeat to Milan prevents anyone from pretending the journey has been uninterrupted triumph. Great teams are measured not by an absence of setbacks but by what they build beyond them.

Before the final, Saladino told reporters that European glory was necessary but not sufficient: Napoli were striving towards a dynasty. He did not claim that one night would finish the project. In fact, he made the opposite argument — that the club's ambition extended beyond any single prize.

He also gave Naples a promise of effort rather than a guarantee of victory. His players, he said, put the crest before the name. The final against Madrid supplied the result he refused to promise, delivered by the young footballers he refused to abandon.

This is why the story cannot be reduced to Madrid losing out on a manager. The greater story is that Napoli refused to behave like a waiting room for somebody else's greatness. In Lisbon, they became European champions on their own terms.

articles.headline: SALADINO: 'WE ARE STRIVING TOWARDS A DYNASTY'
articles.dek: Napoli's manager explains why he rejected Madrid and what comes next.
articles.label: MANAGER PRESS CONFERENCE
body: Stefan Saladino has set his sights beyond a second consecutive Scudetto and a first Champions League final. 'Of course it does. Necessary but not sufficient. We are striving towards a dynasty,' he said when asked whether European glory was needed to complete his Napoli project.

The manager confirmed he had declined an approach from Real Madrid last summer, emphasizing respect for the club but explaining: 'I feel like we’re BUILDING something special here and it’s not done. I need to see it out.'

Repeatedly challenged by Spanish journalists, Saladino insisted the final would neither validate nor invalidate his choice. 'My story is one intertwined with Napoli for the moment,' he told MARCA. He highlighted his commitment to developing Pio Esposito, Mikey Moore and Peacock, rather than treating their growth as a stepping stone to another club.

The sharpest exchange came when El Chiringuito suggested staying in Naples was the safer option. 'I don’t think anyone who cares about whats “safe” would take a job at Napoli to begin with. And they certainly wouldn’t take one with the Azzurri,' Saladino replied.
Despite his enormous ambitions, the manager refused to guarantee a result: 'Results aren’t guaranteed. Effort can be.' That is the standard he wants his players to carry into the final.

articles.headline: THE CREST BEFORE THE NAME: SALADINO'S MESSAGE TO NAPLES
articles.dek: A manager's message to the city ahead of a European final.
articles.label: NAPLES · THE FINAL
body: Saladino's press conference turned emotional when Il Mattino asked what he wanted the people of Naples to know about their players. He spoke of men who live for the shirt and put the crest on the front before the name on the back.
He told supporters that the players share the emotions they feel watching and that the city and the team face this moment together.
His final answer set a simple standard: the players should be able to say they gave their full effort. Results are not guaranteed, he said. Effort can be.
For all the talk of a dynasty, Napoli's manager did not promise the trophy. He asked for commitment, solidarity and everything the squad can give on the pitch.

articles.headline: PIO ESPOSITO TO MADRID PRESS: 'I HAVE TO SHOW YOU ON THE PITCH'
articles.dek: After the Coppa shootout heartbreak, Napoli's 43-goal striker faces the cameras and refuses to hide.
articles.label: PIO ESPOSITO · FINAL MEDIA DAY
body: Pio Esposito did not try to avoid the question. As he sat before the international press ahead of Napoli's Champions League final against Real Madrid, the Coppa Italia shootout against Milan remained fresh. The striker had scored the 90th-minute equalizer that forced extra time, then missed Napoli's only penalty in a 5–4 shootout defeat.

Asked how he had dealt with the disappointment, Esposito replied: 'It hurt. A lot.' He spoke about wanting to win for the club, supporters and teammates, and about believing Napoli could win after his late goal. Then he acknowledged the decisive moment without looking for an excuse: 'Then the penalties came, and I missed mine.'

What followed was a reminder of the mentality required from a striker. 'But I'm a striker. I cannot be afraid of missing,' he told the room. 'If I spend the rest of my career thinking about one penalty, I won't be the player this club needs.'

Esposito has scored 43 goals across all competitions this season. One of them, an 85th-minute finish from Maximilian Beier's through ball in Turin, sent Napoli into this European final. Another rescued the Coppa final in the 90th minute. The missed penalty matters, but it does not describe his season on its own.

A Spanish journalist then asked whether he truly belonged on the same stage as Real Madrid's biggest names. Esposito smiled before delivering the line that will dominate the headlines: 'I don't need to tell you I belong. I have to show you on the pitch.'

There was no promise of a goal, no prediction of a result, and no attempt to manufacture a rivalry. The answer was simpler and more compelling: Esposito understands the pressure and intends to respond through football. Whether he can do so against Real Madrid remains the question of the final.

articles.headline: BEIER ANSWERS MADRID PRESS: ONE SHOOTOUT DOES NOT DEFINE NAPOLI
articles.dek: The forward with 35 goals and 24 assists explains why Napoli's belief survived the Coppa defeat.
articles.label: BEIER · FINAL MEDIA DAY
body: Maximilian Beier arrived at the Champions League final media day with numbers that would dominate the conversation in almost any other week: 35 goals and 24 assists across all competitions. Yet the most pointed question he faced concerned a trophy Napoli had failed to win.

Beier has been at the heart of Napoli's attack, creating as well as finishing. Asked by German reporters whether he had reached a new level, he said he had become 'a more complete player' and explained that he enjoyed creating opportunities for teammates as much as scoring. He cited the quality of Pio Esposito, Olise, Davies and Nico Paz as a reason to keep searching for passes.

The sharpest exchange came from the Spanish press. With Napoli beaten by Milan in the Coppa Italia final despite Beier assisting both goals, a journalist asked whether the defeat exposed a weakness under pressure. Beier rejected the premise. 'No. I don't agree with that,' he replied.

'We lost on penalties. That's football. It hurts, but I don't think you can look at one shootout and decide a team cannot handle pressure.' He pointed directly to the Champions League semifinal: 'Against Juventus, we were behind in the semifinal. We came back. That was pressure too.'

The Turin example is difficult to dispute. With Napoli trailing 1–0 on aggregate, Scott McTominay equalized the tie before Beier's through ball released Esposito for the winner in the 85th minute. The same creative connection produced the 90th-minute equalizer against Milan, though the subsequent shootout ended in defeat.

Beier did not pretend the Coppa loss was painless. Nor did he accept the suggestion that it foretold what would happen against Real Madrid. His answer was grounded in the evidence of Napoli's season: a Scudetto, a comeback in Turin and a team whose attacking partnerships have repeatedly delivered when it mattered.

articles.headline: BASTONI'S MESSAGE TO MADRID: RESPECT, NOT FEAR
articles.dek: Napoli's captain refuses to let Real Madrid's reputation dictate the European final.
articles.label: BASTONI · FINAL MEDIA DAY
body: Alessandro Bastoni sat before the international press with the calm of a captain who has already led Napoli to a second consecutive Serie A title. Ninety-three points, only one league defeat and a place in the Champions League final form the backdrop to his biggest assignment yet: facing Real Madrid.

Asked whether the occasion felt like the biggest of his career, Bastoni answered without hesitation: 'Assolutamente. Yes, of course.' He spoke of childhood dreams and the importance of earning the right to play on a stage like this. But there was nothing deferential about his assessment of the opposition.

'Real Madrid are Real Madrid. We respect their history. But we didn't reach this final by accident,' the captain told reporters. He pointed to the knockout victories over Barcelona and Juventus, particularly the comeback in Turin after Napoli had lost the semifinal first leg.

A Spanish journalist pressed him on whether Madrid's history of winning European finals created fear in the dressing room. Bastoni's answer was a single word: 'No.' Then he expanded: 'Respect? Absolutely. Fear? No.'

The captain credited a message from manager Stefan Saladino before the Coppa Italia final: 'Respect, not fear.' It was a phrase Napoli had needed against Milan, when they twice recovered from falling behind before losing on penalties. Now it has become the public expression of the team's approach to Madrid.

Bastoni offered no prediction and no theatrical promise. His argument was simpler: Napoli earned this final by beating elite opponents, and they intend to compete as equals. For a club seeking its greatest European night, the captain's composure may be as important as the noise around the occasion.

articles.headline: NAPOLI VS REAL MADRID: THE EUROPEAN FINAL
articles.dek: Back-to-back Italian champions prepare for their biggest match.
articles.label: CHAMPIONS LEAGUE FINAL
body: Napoli's season reaches its biggest stage against Real Madrid in the Champions League final. The club finished Serie A with 93 points, 28 wins, nine draws and one defeat, securing a second consecutive league title.

The route here demanded resilience. Napoli overcame Barcelona before overturning a first-leg deficit against Juventus. Scott McTominay scored in Turin and Pio Esposito struck the 85th-minute winner from a Maximilian Beier pass.

The Coppa Italia ended painfully against Milan on penalties after Esposito's 90th-minute equalizer. Now Napoli have another final to play. Meret and Kayode's fitness remains uncertain; the lineup and kickoff details have not been confirmed.
Real Madrid's European reputation needs no introduction. Napoli have earned their place through results. The trophy will be decided on the pitch, not by the weight of history.

articles.headline: BEIER AND ESPOSITO: NAPOLI'S BIGGEST WEAPONS
articles.dek: Two forwards, 78 combined goals and a European final ahead.
articles.label: FINAL PLAYER FOCUS
body: Maximilian Beier enters the European final buildup with 35 goals and 24 assists across all competitions. Pio Esposito has 43 goals. Together they have been at the centre of Napoli's biggest moments.
In Turin, Beier's through ball released Esposito for the 85th-minute winner against Juventus. In the Coppa final, Beier assisted both Napoli goals, including Esposito's 90th-minute equalizer.

The penalty Esposito missed against Milan will follow him into this final's buildup. But the same striker scored the goal that sent Napoli to extra time and the goal that sent them into the Champions League final.
Against Real Madrid, Napoli need both men confident, connected and ready to take their chances.

articles.headline: THE TACTICAL BATTLE: NAPOLI'S ROUTE THROUGH MADRID
articles.dek: Midfield control, defensive transitions and the selection questions that matter.
articles.label: TACTICAL PREVIEW
body: The Champions League final is a contest of moments as much as systems. Napoli must manage the spaces behind their fullbacks, protect the central areas and resist the temptation to force every attack.
João Neves provides an important midfield foundation. Scott McTominay demonstrated against Juventus how a midfielder can turn a European tie with one decisive run and finish.

Bastoni and Buongiorno have formed a defensive foundation for a team that conceded just 17 goals in Serie A. With Kayode's availability uncertain, the right-back position remains a selection question. Calafiori has covered there while Cucurella operates on the left.

Meret's recovery is also uncertain, and Peacock has already been tested in the Coppa final. The coaching staff have not confirmed their selection. Napoli's challenge is to be bold in possession and disciplined without it.

articles.headline: MILAN WIN COPPA ON PENALTIES AFTER PIO'S LATE RESCUE
articles.dek: A dramatic 2–2 final ends in Milan's 5–4 shootout victory. Esposito equalizes in the 90th minute but misses his penalty.
articles.label: COPPA ITALIA FINAL · MILAN WIN 5–4 ON PENS
body: AC Milan have won the Coppa Italia after a dramatic final against Napoli finished 2–2 after extra time and 5–4 in the penalty shootout. Pio Esposito's 90th-minute equalizer rescued Napoli from defeat in regulation, but he was the only player to miss in a shootout in which Milan converted all five attempts.

Napoli's young deputy goalkeeper Peacock kept the first half scoreless with two important stops. In the 23rd minute he saved a header following a Milan cross, and another good save followed before the interval. Michael Olise narrowly missed an opportunity for Napoli.

Roony opened the scoring for Milan in the 48th minute. Davies equalized in the 58th after a pass from Maximilian Beier, but Giménez restored Milan's lead in the 63rd. Napoli were still trailing at the 90-minute mark when Beier found Esposito inside the box. The striker received the ball, established position, turned and finished to make it 2–2.

Neither side scored in extra time. The penalties were unforgiving: Milan scored five, Napoli four. Esposito, the man who had kept Napoli alive with his late equalizer, missed Napoli's only kick. Milan lifted the trophy; Napoli were left with a defeat that was both deservedly recorded and desperately painful.

Beier supplied both Napoli goals, bringing his all-competition assist tally to 24 alongside 35 goals. Esposito's equalizer was his 43rd goal of the season. The Scudetto has already been secured, but the domestic double is now beyond reach. Napoli must regroup for their Champions League final against Real Madrid.

articles.headline: PIO SAVED THE FINAL BEFORE HIS PENALTY BROKE NAPOLI HEARTS
articles.dek: The striker's 90th-minute goal made the shootout possible. His miss decided it.
articles.label: PIO · HEROISM AND HEARTBREAK
body: The last image of Pio Esposito's Coppa Italia final is a missed penalty. It cannot be the only image. At the 90th minute, with Napoli trailing Milan 2–1, he received Maximilian Beier's pass in the penalty area, found his position, turned and scored. That finish saved Napoli from defeat in regulation.

The goal forced another thirty minutes. Neither side scored in extra time. In the shootout Milan converted five penalties, Napoli four, and Esposito was the only taker to miss. His kick mattered; the result cannot be explained away. But without his goal ten minutes earlier, Napoli would never have reached penalties.

Esposito's 43rd goal of the season was a reminder of how often he has carried Napoli's attack. His missed kick was a reminder of how cruel a final can be. The two moments must be remembered together. The loss belongs to a team that conceded twice and could not find a winner across 120 minutes, not to one player alone.

The season still holds a Champions League final against Real Madrid. Esposito will have to face the disappointment, but his teammates and supporters should remember who kept the Coppa dream alive until the last possible stage.

articles.headline: TWO SAVES, TWO ASSISTS: PEACOCK AND BEIER DESERVED MORE
articles.dek: The backup keeper kept Napoli alive early; Beier created both equalizers.
articles.label: COPPA FINAL · PLAYER FOCUS
body: Peacock's Coppa Italia final began with a significant test. In the 23rd minute a Milan cross found a head, and Napoli's young goalkeeper made a big save. Another good stop followed before halftime. Called upon because of Alex Meret's injury, Peacock helped his side reach the interval level.

Milan scored twice after the break, and all five Milan penalty takers converted in the shootout. That does not erase the saves Peacock made. A goalkeeper can be beaten from the spot without having let his team down. His first-half contribution was real and measurable.

Maximilian Beier, meanwhile, assisted both Napoli goals. He found Davies for the 58th-minute equalizer, then supplied Pio Esposito's dramatic 90th-minute finish. His season totals now stand at 35 goals and 24 assists across all competitions.

The headlines will rightly belong to Milan's cup triumph and Esposito's missed penalty. But the final was also shaped by a young goalkeeper answering the call and a forward who created two separate comebacks. Napoli's next challenge is to carry those performances into the European final.

articles.headline: THE DOUBLE IS GONE. MADRID IS STILL WAITING.
articles.dek: Napoli have lost the Coppa Italia final, but their biggest match is still ahead.
articles.label: EDITORIAL · WHAT COMES NEXT
body: The treble is no longer possible. AC Milan won the Coppa Italia final, defeating Napoli 5–4 on penalties after a 2–2 draw. That is the result, and Milan deserve their moment. For Napoli the disappointment is severe precisely because the chance to win a second trophy was so close.

Yet this team are already back-to-back Serie A champions. They overturned a Champions League semifinal deficit against Juventus in Turin and earned a place in the final against Real Madrid. The Coppa defeat changes the trophy count, not the achievements that brought Napoli to this point.

There will be questions about Pio Esposito's penalty, about defensive lapses after halftime, and about the injury-hit goalkeeper situation. They deserve calm analysis rather than public scapegoating. Esposito scored the goal that forced extra time. Peacock made two important first-half saves. Beier assisted both goals. None of those facts disappears because the shootout went Milan's way.

The next European final is not a consolation match. It is the biggest challenge still available. The date and team selection remain unconfirmed here; the club must prepare without inventing answers about Meret or Kayode's fitness. Napoli have no time to dwell, but they do have time to learn.
Milan have their cup. Napoli have their league crown and a date with Real Madrid. The final chapter of this season has not yet been written.

articles.headline: CAMPIONI ANCORA: NAPOLI RETAIN THE SCUDETTO
articles.dek: Beier scores twice against Lecce as Napoli clinch the championship with two matches remaining.
articles.label: NAPOLI 2–0 LECCE · CHAMPIONS
body: The full-time whistle confirmed what Napoli had spent an entire season working toward. Champions of Italy again. A 2–0 victory over Lecce took the club to 89 points from 36 matches, an unassailable total with two league fixtures still to play. This was no last-day escape. Napoli had built a lead large enough to finish the race early.

Maximilian Beier struck in the 20th minute from Nico Paz's assist. At halftime the score remained 1–0, a lead that was valuable but fragile. In the 77th minute Kevin De Bruyne provided the pass for Beier's second goal. The brace delivered the victory and the title. Beier now leads Serie A with 27 goals, ahead of Kenan Yıldız on 25 and Pio Esposito on 23.

The championship came amid a difficult injury spell. Starting goalkeeper Alex Meret and right-back Michael Kayode are both sidelined for around three weeks. Peacock stepped into goal and recorded a clean sheet on the day the Scudetto was clinched. His contribution belongs in the championship story, not merely in a footnote.

Napoli have now retained their league crown while reaching the Coppa Italia final against AC Milan and the Champions League final against Real Madrid. Neither cup has been won. But the first trophy of this extraordinary run-in is secure. Eighty-nine points. Two games left. Campioni ancora.

articles.headline: NINE CLEAN SHEETS IN FOURTEEN: GIVE PEACOCK HIS FLOWERS
articles.dek: The backup goalkeeper was asked to help clinch the Scudetto. He answered with another shutout.
articles.label: PEACOCK · THE SCUDETTO KEEPER
body: A backup goalkeeper can spend an entire season being judged by what he might not be able to do. Peacock deserves to be judged by what he has actually done. Fourteen Serie A appearances. Nine clean sheets. A remarkable 64.3 percent shutout rate. And now a clean sheet in the match that secured Napoli's second consecutive Scudetto.

For perspective, Alex Meret has 12 clean sheets in 22 league appearances. Unai Simón has 12 in 36. Svilar and Di Gregorio each have 10 in 36. Clean sheets belong to entire defensive units, and different opponents create different challenges. Still, Peacock's record cannot be dismissed simply because he is rated 74 overall.

With Meret sidelined for approximately three weeks, Peacock was entrusted with the goal against Lecce. Napoli needed one victory to make the championship mathematical. Beier supplied the goals, one assisted by Nico Paz and the other by Kevin De Bruyne. Peacock supplied the clean sheet. That is exactly what was asked of him.

There is no reason to pretend Lecce posed the same challenge as Real Madrid, or to invent spectacular saves that were never reported. The significance lies in the responsibility and the result. On the day Napoli became champions, Peacock was the goalkeeper who saw them across the line.

His next assignment is confirmed: AC Milan in the Coppa Italia final on May 9. He might also face Real Madrid in the Champions League final if Meret is not ready. Neither final has happened yet. But this title is real, his nine clean sheets are real, and his contribution to the Scudetto is already part of Napoli history. Give him his flowers.

articles.headline: BEIER'S DOUBLE DELIVERS THE TITLE: 27 LEAGUE GOALS AND COUNTING
articles.dek: Nico Paz and Kevin De Bruyne supply the assists as Napoli's leading scorer seals the Scudetto.
articles.label: BEIER · 20′ AND 77′
body: A title-winning season contains many decisive goals, but few players get the opportunity to score twice in the match that mathematically seals the championship. Maximilian Beier took that opportunity against Lecce. In the 20th minute he scored from Nico Paz's assist. In the 77th, Kevin De Bruyne found him for a second. Napoli won 2–0 and became champions with two games to spare.

The double carried Beier to 27 Serie A goals, two clear of Kenan Yıldız and four ahead of teammate Pio Esposito. The Golden Boot race is not finished, but Beier's place at the centre of Napoli's title triumph is assured. Across all competitions he now has 35 goals.

The two assists also told a story of Napoli's creative depth. Nico Paz helped establish the lead; the 37-year-old De Bruyne helped secure it. The goalscorer will dominate the images of the day, rightly, but neither finish happened in isolation.

This was a championship-clinching brace, not merely another statistical contribution. Beier gave Napoli the result they needed, and when the referee blew for full time, the league table could no longer be contested.

articles.headline: CHAMPIONS ALREADY. MILAN NEXT. MADRID WAITING.
articles.dek: Napoli celebrate the Scudetto while preparing for two finals and monitoring two crucial injuries.
articles.label: THE ROAD AHEAD
body: The Scudetto has been won. Napoli have 89 points with two Serie A matches remaining. Their next challenge is not to prove they are champions of Italy, but to see how much more this remarkable season can hold.

AC Milan await in the Coppa Italia final on May 9. Real Madrid await in the Champions League final after Napoli's extraordinary 2–0 semifinal victory away at Juventus. The European comeback was secured by Scott McTominay's 51st-minute equaliser and Pio Esposito's 85th-minute winner.

The injury situation complicates the plans. Meret and Kayode are each expected to miss approximately three weeks, making their availability for Madrid uncertain. Peacock will start against Milan. Calafiori provides an option at right-back while Cucurella can remain on the left.
For now, no result in either final can be assumed. The Scudetto is the first confirmed prize. The remaining matches will determine whether this championship season becomes something even larger.

articles.headline: BELLANDI: JUVENTUS HAD THE ADVANTAGE. NAPOLI HAD THE ANSWER.
articles.dek: The first leg suggested Juventus knew how to stop Napoli. Turin supplied a devastating rebuttal.
articles.label: BELLANDI · AFTER THE COMEBACK
body: It is easy to sound wise after the final whistle, so let us start with what was true before it: Juventus won the first leg in Naples 1–0. Kenan Yıldız scored in the 74th minute. Napoli did not respond. The home defeat placed their European ambitions in genuine jeopardy, and there was no guarantee that the return would be any kinder.

At halftime in Turin, the hosts still led the tie. Napoli's 72 percent possession and three shots on target were encouraging, but they were not a result. Football has never awarded semifinal places for possession. The visitors still needed the goal they had failed to find in Naples.

Then came Scott McTominay. His 51st-minute run across the penalty area and top-corner finish, assisted by João Neves, did more than equalise the aggregate score. It gave the evening a new direction. The advantage Juventus had defended across the first leg and the opening half of the second was gone.

The decisive blow came in the 85th minute, when Maximilian Beier sent Pio Esposito through and the striker finished. A tie that Juventus had led for so long ended with Napoli winning 2–1 on aggregate. There is no need to invent dressing-room speeches or imaginary controversies to make this dramatic. The sequence speaks for itself.

I questioned whether Napoli could turn control into a European knockout result. In Turin, they answered. They did it with patience, individual quality and two goals of very different character. The next opponent is Real Madrid, and another formidable examination awaits. Tonight, however, the verdict belongs to Napoli.

articles.headline: ONE WIN FROM THE SCUDETTO. TWO FINALS AHEAD. AND NOW AN INJURY CRISIS.
articles.dek: The Turin triumph opens a path to three trophies, but injuries to Meret and Kayode test Napoli's depth.
articles.label: THE RUN-IN · THREE FRONTS
body: Napoli have reached the Champions League final against Real Madrid by defeating Juventus 2–0 in Turin, overturning a one-goal first-leg deficit. The result is enormous on its own. Placed alongside the rest of the season, it becomes almost difficult to comprehend.

In Serie A, Napoli hold 86 points from 35 matches. Roma are seven behind and Juventus eight behind. One more Napoli league victory guarantees the Scudetto. The Coppa Italia final against AC Milan is set for May 9. Now there is a Champions League final as well. Three fronts remain alive; no trophy has yet been secured.

Yet the celebrations in Turin have been followed by serious medical news. Goalkeeper Alex Meret and right-back Michael Kayode are each expected to miss approximately three weeks. Both may recover in time for the Champions League final, but neither is certain to be available.

That makes Peacock, the 74-rated backup goalkeeper, an unexpectedly central figure in the run-in. He is expected to play the Coppa Italia final and will be called upon as Napoli attempt to clinch the league. Depending on Meret's recovery, he may also face Real Madrid. At right-back, Calafiori can step into the side while Cucurella remains on the left, preserving the broader defensive structure.

The team that reached the final was built on elite individual performances, from McTominay's spectacular equaliser to Esposito's 85th-minute winner. The team that tries to finish the season with silverware may need equally important contributions from its reserves.
This is the tension at the heart of Napoli's extraordinary spring: unprecedented opportunity, immediate uncertainty, and a set of matches that will decide how the season is remembered.

articles.headline: FROM ONE EDGE OF THE BOX TO THE OTHER: THE GOAL THAT BROKE JUVENTUS
articles.dek: Scott McTominay turned 45 minutes of territorial dominance into one spectacular equaliser.
articles.label: 51′ · MCTOMINAY · ASSIST NEVES
body: There are goals that alter a scoreline, and there are goals that alter the emotional temperature of an entire semifinal. Scott McTominay's 51st-minute strike in Turin belonged unmistakably to the second category. Napoli arrived trailing 1–0 from the first leg. They spent the first half with the ball, generating openings, but Juventus went into the interval still protecting that precious advantage.

The halftime statistics were striking: 72 percent Napoli possession, three shots on target to Juventus's one. Yet there was a cruel simplicity to the situation. All that control had not changed the aggregate score. The visitors needed someone to turn pressure into a goal, and McTominay decided to do it himself.

João Neves provided the assist. McTominay carried the ball from one edge of the penalty area to the other, then unleashed a shot into the top corner. The finish was spectacular, but the run before it mattered just as much: direct, assertive, refusing to allow the match to remain a story of missed opportunity.

At 1–1 on aggregate, Napoli were no longer chasing Juventus's lead. They were chasing the winner. That distinction changed the second half's stakes. The home side's first-leg advantage had vanished, and the tie was open again.

Pio Esposito would seize the decisive moment in the 85th minute, finishing Maximilian Beier's through ball. That is the goal that sent Napoli through. But the comeback had two essential acts. McTominay wrote the first, and without it the final scene could not have happened.

When Napoli remember the night they conquered Turin, they will remember the striker racing clear late on. They should also remember the midfielder who looked at an increasingly desperate situation and answered with a shot into the top corner.

articles.headline: THE PASS BEFORE THE PANDEMONIUM: HOW BEIER FOUND PIO
articles.dek: A perfectly timed through ball and an unflinching finish decided the semifinal.
articles.label: 85′ · BEIER ASSISTS ESPOSITO
body: A great finish is often remembered as a solitary act. The forward runs, the goalkeeper waits, the ball crosses the line, and history assigns a name to the moment. But Napoli's 85th-minute winner in Turin belonged to two players. Maximilian Beier made the opening. Pio Esposito completed it.

With the aggregate score level at 1–1, Beier slipped the ball through to Esposito, who broke clear alone. It was an extraordinary decision under extraordinary pressure: the right pass at the right moment, delivered when an entire Champions League semifinal could still swing either way.

Esposito's task was brutally simple and impossibly difficult. One chance. One finish. The possibility of a European final waiting on the other side. He scored, turning the tie from a stalemate into a 2–1 Napoli aggregate lead.

The combination also tells a larger story about Napoli's attack. Beier had scored 33 goals across competitions entering this match, while Esposito had reached 41 before Turin. They are not merely two players taking turns to finish moves. Their understanding can create the decisive chance even when the game is tight and the margin for error has almost disappeared.

It would be easy to focus exclusively on the strike. Yet the pass is what made the finish possible. That is not a claim about unreported defensive movement or invented buildup: the confirmed sequence is powerful enough on its own. Beier slipped it through. Esposito ran alone. Esposito scored.

There are seasons remembered for a league table and seasons remembered for one piece of football. Napoli may end up with both. In Turin, the decisive piece of football lasted only a few seconds, but it will outlive the night.

articles.headline: 85 MINUTES. ONE PASS. ONE FINISH. NAPOLI ARE IN THE FINAL
articles.dek: An 85th-minute connection between Beier and Esposito completes Napoli's comeback in Turin.
articles.label: JUVENTUS 0–2 NAPOLI · AGGREGATE 1–2
body: For eighty-four minutes, the Champions League semifinal had demanded patience. Juventus had carried a one-goal advantage into the second leg, Napoli had dominated much of the ball, and Scott McTominay had dragged the visitors level on aggregate with a strike of startling quality. Yet the tie remained balanced. One moment could decide which club would walk into the final. In the 85th minute, that moment arrived.

Maximilian Beier slipped a through ball into the path of Pio Esposito. The striker was running alone, facing the opportunity every forward imagines and almost nobody experiences: a chance to send his club to a Champions League final. There was no hesitation in the finish. Esposito scored, and the arithmetic flipped. Napoli were suddenly leading 2–1 across the two legs.

The first half had ended 0–0 despite Napoli controlling 72 percent of possession and registering three shots on target to Juventus's one. Those numbers described pressure, but they offered no consolation while the hosts still held the aggregate lead. Then, six minutes after the restart, João Neves supplied McTominay, whose drive across the area ended with a spectacular shot into the top corner.

McTominay's equaliser gave Napoli the platform. Beier's pass and Esposito's finish provided the verdict. The final whistle confirmed a 2–0 away win and a 2–1 aggregate triumph, turning the pain of a 1–0 first-leg home defeat into a defining European comeback.

Esposito's goal was his 42nd of the season in all competitions. Numbers can capture his output, but not the weight of this particular finish. At 85 minutes in Turin, a prolific campaign acquired its signature moment. Napoli will face Real Madrid in the Champions League final.

articles.headline: MERET'S MASTERCLASS, BEIER'S WINNER: NAPOLI CONQUER INTER
articles.dek: Beier finishes Pio Esposito's assist in the 63rd minute, but Alex Meret's outstanding display is just as decisive in a 1–0 victory.
articles.label: INTER 0–1 NAPOLI · FULL-TIME
body: Napoli left Inter with three points and a clean sheet after Maximilian Beier struck in the 63rd minute from a Pio Esposito assist. The 1–0 victory moved Napoli to 86 points with three Serie A matches remaining.

For all the focus on Napoli's prolific forward pairing, this was a night for Alex Meret. The goalkeeper delivered a massive performance to preserve the lead and make Beier's goal stand up as the winner. The exact number of saves was not confirmed, but the importance of his contribution was unmistakable.

Beier's goal was his 33rd of the season across all competitions, while Pio's assist took his running tally to 23. Napoli's league record now reads 26 wins, eight draws and just one defeat in 35 matches.
Roma and Juventus both won their Matchday 35 fixtures. Napoli remain seven points ahead of Roma and eight ahead of Juventus. One more league victory guarantees the title.

articles.headline: ONE WIN FROM IMMORTALITY: NAPOLI STAND ON THE BRINK OF THE SCUDETTO
articles.dek: Thirty-five matches. Twenty-six wins. One defeat. A seven-point lead over Roma. Napoli now control their own coronation.
articles.label: SCUDETTO WATCH · THREE MATCHES REMAIN
body: The mathematics are finally simple. Napoli have 86 points from 35 matches, Roma have 79 and Juventus 78. With three rounds left, one more Napoli victory would put them on 89 points — beyond Roma's maximum possible 88.

Napoli's 1–0 win at Inter was not a rout or a procession. Maximilian Beier's 63rd-minute goal, assisted by Pio Esposito, decided the contest, while Alex Meret's exceptional goalkeeping protected the narrow advantage.
Roma and Juventus each collected three points in Matchday 35, ensuring the gap stayed at seven and eight points respectively. The pursuit has been relentless, but the leaders have matched it.
There is still work to do. Napoli have not yet clinched the championship. But after 35 games and only one defeat, the next win would end the argument.

articles.headline: BELLANDI: DON'T CROWN NAPOLI YET — THE HARDEST THREE POINTS ARE STILL TO COME
articles.dek: Meret rescued the night, Beier delivered the winner, and Napoli have one more hurdle before the champagne.
articles.label: BELLANDI · TITLE RACE
body: Seven points ahead of Roma. Three matches to play. Napoli supporters are entitled to dream, but the title has not yet been awarded.

The 1–0 win over Inter offered a reminder that the final stretch can be uncomfortable. Beier scored in the 63rd minute from Pio Esposito's assist; Meret was outstanding in keeping the advantage intact. Without the goalkeeper's contribution, this could have been a very different evening.

Napoli's record of 26 wins, eight draws and one loss is extraordinary. So is the pressure that comes with standing one victory away from the Scudetto. Roma are still winning. Juventus are still winning. Nobody is handing the leaders anything.

The arithmetic favours Napoli overwhelmingly. The dressing room, however, must deal in performances, not celebrations. Win once more and nobody can catch them. Until then, the story remains unfinished.

articles.headline: THE OTHER MATCH-WINNER: WHY MERET DESERVES HIS OWN HEADLINE
articles.dek: A clean sheet alone doesn't tell the story of Napoli's 1–0 win over Inter. Meret's influence was fundamental.
articles.label: ALEX MERET · INTER 0–1 NAPOLI
body: The scoreline will always show one scorer: Maximilian Beier, 63 minutes. The assist belongs to Pio Esposito. But the defining story of Napoli's narrow victory over Inter has another name: Alex Meret.
Meret was massive. In a match decided by a single goal, his outstanding work in goal protected the result and ensured Napoli departed with a clean sheet and all three points.
No save count or individual sequence is being attributed without confirmation. The assessment is simpler, and stronger: Napoli's goalkeeper was one of the principal reasons the team won.
For a squad now one victory away from the Serie A title, that contribution deserves equal billing with the finish at the other end.

articles.headline: YILDIZ STRIKES AS JUVENTUS TAKE ONE-GOAL LEAD TO TURIN
articles.dek: Kenan Yıldız's 74th-minute goal leaves Napoli trailing 1–0 after the Champions League semifinal first leg.
articles.label: NAPOLI 0–1 JUVENTUS · FIRST LEG
body: Napoli's Champions League semifinal began with a home defeat as Kenan Yıldız scored in the 74th minute to give Juventus a 1–0 first-leg victory at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.
The opening half ended goalless. Napoli carried attacking intent but could not turn their pressure into a breakthrough, leaving the tie delicately balanced at the interval.
The decisive moment arrived with sixteen minutes of regulation time remaining. Yıldız scored for Juventus, and Napoli were unable to find an equaliser before the final whistle.
The result leaves Napoli needing to overturn a one-goal deficit in the second leg away to Juventus on May 2. The tie is not settled, but the advantage belongs to the visitors after ninety minutes.
Napoli remain top of Serie A on 83 points after 34 matches and have a Coppa Italia final against AC Milan on May 9. Their pursuit of three trophies has encountered its most immediate setback yet.

articles.headline: ONE GOAL DOWN, NINETY MINUTES LEFT: WHAT NAPOLI MUST CHANGE IN TURIN
articles.dek: The first-half threat was not enough. Napoli must turn possession and movement into goals away from home.
articles.label: UCL SEMIFINAL · RETURN LEG MAY 2
body: The scoreline is stark: Napoli 0, Juventus 1. Yet the margin is small enough that the Champions League semifinal remains open ahead of the return in Turin.
Napoli appeared the more dangerous side in stretches of the first half, but no breakthrough arrived. That distinction matters: creating threatening situations and finishing them are different tasks.

Pio Esposito entered the tie with 41 goals across all competitions, while Maximilian Beier had 32. Their season-long output is undeniable, but Juventus prevented Napoli from scoring in the opening leg.

A return leg away from home creates competing demands. Napoli must score, but conceding again would increase the deficit. The balance between attacking urgency and protection against transitions will be central.
The next ninety minutes will decide whether Napoli's European campaign continues. A single goal would level the aggregate score; anything beyond that depends on how the second leg unfolds.

articles.headline: BELLANDI: JUVENTUS HAVE DONE WHAT THE LEAGUE TABLE SAID THEY COULDN'T
articles.dek: A goal from Yıldız flips the mood of the semifinal and asks uncomfortable questions of Napoli's finishing.
articles.label: BELLANDI · EUROPEAN VERDICT
body: Eight points separate Napoli and Juventus in Serie A. On the Champions League scoreboard, Juventus lead 1–0. That is why knockout football refuses to obey the league table.

Napoli came into this semifinal after scoring four against Lazio and four against Torino. At home against Juventus, the attack failed to register a goal. Kenan Yıldız supplied the only finish that mattered.

There is no need to manufacture a crisis around one defeat. Napoli have been exceptional domestically and remain in contention for multiple trophies. But a European semifinal is not won on accumulated league form.
Juventus can now defend an advantage in front of their own supporters on May 2. Napoli must find a way to impose their attacking quality without allowing the tie to run away from them.
The next leg will tell us whether this was merely a setback or the night Napoli's European ambition began to unravel. The difference is still just one goal.

articles.headline: YILDIZ AFTER THE WIN: 'ONE GOAL DOESN'T SEND YOU TO A FINAL'
articles.dek: Juventus's match-winner reflects on a narrow first-leg advantage and the challenge still ahead.
articles.label: THE INTERVIEW · KENAN YILDIZ
body: Marco Rinaldi: You scored the only goal in Naples. What does that mean in a Champions League semifinal?
Kenan Yıldız: 'It means we have an advantage, and that's important. But one goal doesn't send you to a final. We still have another match to play.'
Rinaldi: Napoli were dangerous in the first half. How difficult was it to stay patient?
Yıldız: 'You have to accept that there will be moments when the other team has the ball and pushes you back. We kept believing there would be a chance for us.'
Rinaldi: Juventus are eight points behind Napoli in the league. Does this result change how you see the rivalry?
Yıldız: 'The league and this competition are different. We respect Napoli. Tonight we did our job, and now we have to do it again at home.'
Rinaldi: What will decide the second leg?
Yıldız: 'Details. The same as tonight. If we think the work is finished, we'll make a mistake.'

articles.headline: FOUR MORE FOR NAPOLI: TORINO BEATEN AS TITLE COUNTDOWN CONTINUES
articles.dek: Esposito, McTominay and Beier score in a 4–1 home win; a Sazonov own goal completes the tally.
articles.label: NAPOLI 4–1 TORINO · 83 POINTS
body: Napoli moved to 83 points with a 4–1 home victory over Torino, maintaining a seven-point advantage over Roma with four Serie A matches remaining.

Pio Esposito opened the scoring after 13 minutes from Nico Paz's pass. Torino levelled in the 23rd through Díaz, who reacted after goalkeeper Peacock had made the initial save in a goalmouth scramble.

Napoli restored the lead in the 30th minute when Esposito's effort from outside the box deflected off Sazonov and went in. The goal was officially recorded as an own goal, leaving Esposito with one credited goal on the night.
Scott McTominay made it 3–1 in the 73rd minute, assisted by Mikey Moore, before Kevin De Bruyne set up Maximilian Beier for Napoli's fourth in the 79th.

Roma and Juventus also won, leaving the top three on 83, 76 and 75 points. Napoli need six more points to guarantee the Scudetto outright, but attention now turns to the Champions League semifinal against Juventus.

articles.headline: ITALY'S BIGGEST EUROPEAN NIGHT: NAPOLI HOST JUVENTUS IN SEMIFINAL FIRST LEG
articles.dek: April 24 at the Maradona. A place in the Champions League final hangs over a rivalry already defining Serie A.
articles.label: APR 24 · NAPOLI vs JUVENTUS · UCL SEMIFINAL
body: The Champions League semifinal begins at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona on April 24, with Napoli welcoming Juventus for the first of two legs that will decide which Italian club reaches the final.

Napoli arrive after eliminating Barcelona 2–1 on aggregate and beating Torino 4–1 in Serie A. Juventus are third domestically on 75 points, eight behind Napoli, but the league table offers no advantage once the European whistle sounds.
The return leg is scheduled for May 2 away to Juventus. Napoli also have a Coppa Italia final against AC Milan on May 9, making this an unusually consequential period for the club.

The attacking numbers are formidable: Pio Esposito has 41 goals in the tracked season tally, while Maximilian Beier has 32. Nico Paz, Michael Olise, João Neves and Kevin De Bruyne give Napoli different routes to create chances.
Juventus will have their own ambitions and a full tie to play. The first-leg task for Napoli is to establish an advantage without mistaking home momentum for a place already secured in the final.

articles.headline: PIO ESPOSITO, ONE-ON-ONE: 'THE BIGGEST NIGHTS ARE THE ONES YOU WORK FOR'
articles.dek: The Napoli striker discusses his partnership with Beier, the 40-goal milestone and the challenge of facing Juventus.
articles.label: THE INTERVIEW · PIO ESPOSITO
body: Giulia Romano: You scored a hat-trick against Lazio and then opened the scoring against Torino. Does the run change how you approach Juventus?

Pio Esposito: 'Not really. You can feel confident, of course, but the next defender doesn't care what you did last week. You have to make the run again, get into the right position again. That's the job.'
Romano: Your understanding with Maximilian Beier has become one of Napoli's defining partnerships. What makes it work?

Esposito: 'Sometimes he sees a space before I do. Sometimes I know he'll make the pass before he gets the ball. We talk a lot on the pitch. And when he's the one running in behind, I have to be ready to find him too.'
Romano: Forty-one goals in all competitions. Do you think about the number?
Esposito: 'My family might count them more than I do. It's nice, obviously. But we're still playing for things. If we reach the final, that's something we'll remember together.'
Romano: Juventus come to Naples for a European semifinal. What does that mean to you?
Esposito: 'You feel what this stadium means before you even walk out. I don't want to promise anything. I just want us to play our football and give the people a night they deserve.'

articles.headline: BEIER ON THE JUVENTUS TEST: 'THE FIRST LEG CANNOT BE THE WHOLE STORY'
articles.dek: After scoring against Torino, the forward reflects on his partnership with Esposito and the discipline needed over two legs.
articles.label: THE INTERVIEW · MAXIMILIAN BEIER
body: Sara Ferraro: Another goal against Torino, this time from Kevin De Bruyne's assist. How much do those different creators change the way you play?

Maximilian Beier: 'It makes my job easier and harder. Easier because the passes can come from everywhere. Harder because I have to stay switched on every second. Kevin can see a run you didn't even know you were making.'
Ferraro: Pio has just passed 40 goals, and you have 32. Is there competition between you?
Beier: 'Of course we want to score. Every striker does. But when Pio scores, that's good for me too. Defenders start looking at him, and maybe I find space. We push each other.'
Ferraro: Juventus are eight points behind in Serie A. Does that matter in Europe?
Beier: 'No. It means we have done well in the league, nothing more. We play them twice, and the first match cannot be the whole story. We have to be smart.'
Ferraro: What do you expect from the Maradona on April 24?
Beier: 'Noise. A lot of it. You feel it when you warm up. The important thing is to use that energy and not get carried away.'

articles.headline: BELLANDI: EIGHT POINTS BEHIND? JUVENTUS CAN STILL RUIN NAPOLI'S EUROPEAN DREAM
articles.dek: The pundit argues that domestic superiority will mean nothing if Napoli lose control of the semifinal.
articles.label: BELLANDI · THE EUROPEAN VERDICT
body: Napoli are the better Serie A side by the standings: 83 points from 34 matches against Juventus's 75. But a Champions League semifinal does not award a head start for league position.

The hosts have scored eight goals in their last two matches, four against Lazio and four against Torino. Pio Esposito and Maximilian Beier are in productive form, and Kevin De Bruyne continues to create decisive moments.

Yet Napoli conceded in both of those victories. That does not establish a defensive crisis, but it is a reminder that one untidy moment can alter a knockout tie, particularly with a second leg still to come in Turin.
