body: NAPLES — João Neves shoots. Bologna block it. Maximilian Beier is there. The sequence took only a moment, but it captured one of the most valuable instincts in the sport: the belief that even a blocked shot is still a scoring opportunity.

Beier's 85th-minute goal gave Napoli a 2–1 victory over Bologna on Christmas Eve, five minutes after Openda had levelled the match. The rebound finish is credited without an assist, despite the preceding shot from Neves.
It also took Beier to nineteen goals and seven assists for Napoli in the 2028–29 club campaign across all competitions. Those are not theoretical contributions; they are shaping results.

Consider the recent sequence. At Lazio on December 9, Beier scored in the 16th and 66th minutes, from Nico Paz and Pio Esposito assists, to secure a 2–1 league victory. At Palermo on December 17, he scored in the 86th from Anton Stach's pass to rescue a 2–2 draw.
Bologna was different. No through ball and no traditional final pass. The keeper of the narrative was the loose ball after a blocked Neves effort. Beier was the quickest to respond.

The striker is far more than a finisher who waits passively in a penalty area. His recent goals show different ways of affecting a match: connections with team-mates, awareness of second balls, and the ability to respond when a game seems to be moving away from Napoli.

These moments do not excuse the team's defensive issues. Indeed, their frequency is partly a symptom of how often Napoli's margin becomes uncomfortable. The brilliance of one player should not become a substitute for control.

But Beier's form provides something precious for a side competing on multiple fronts: conviction that one more chance can be enough. Pio Esposito brings a different dimension with thirteen goals and twelve assists, demonstrating the squad's depth of attacking contribution.

The next listed fixture is the December 29 Supercoppa against Milano FC, the game alias for AC Milan. Its result is not yet known. January will then bring six league dates and two Champions League trips.
Nineteen goals by Christmas Eve, and perhaps the most revealing one arrived only because the first shot did not go in. Beier doesn't appear to stop believing until the ball is dead.

articles.label: SERIE A · PALERMO 2–2 NAPOLI · FULL TIME
articles.imageCredit: Maximilian Beier in Napoli colours · archive player portrait; not an image of the Palermo match
articles.headline: SIX SAVES. TWO COMEBACKS. ONE POINT. NAPOLI ESCAPE PALERMO.
articles.dek: Bottom-of-the-table Palermo go ahead twice through Diakité. Peacock stops six shots before halftime, Olise changes the match, and Beier equalises in the 86th — but the champions cannot escape with all three points.
body: PALERMO, 17 DECEMBER 2028 — A point rescued, two dropped. Napoli left Sicily with a 2–2 draw against a Palermo side at the foot of Serie A, and there was little consolation in the number beside the defending champions' name in the table.

The first half was difficult to watch for the visiting supporters. Young goalkeeper Peacock made SIX saves in the opening forty-five minutes, an extraordinary workload against the last-place team. Palermo repeatedly reached shooting positions and dictated too much of the play.
Diakité gave Palermo the lead in the 29th minute. Despite their goalkeeper's heroics, Napoli went into halftime trailing 1–0 and facing serious questions about their control of the game.

The response began at the interval. Michael Olise and Alphonso Davies were introduced, changing Napoli's attacking energy. A succession of chances followed, and the visitors started to look far more like a side capable of winning the title.
At 60 minutes, Olise supplied the final pass for Scott McTominay's equaliser. Napoli had found their rhythm, but parity did not lead to composure at the other end.

On a counterattack in the 75th minute, Diakité struck again. Palermo led 2–1 with fifteen minutes remaining, and Napoli were once more forced to rescue a match against a team they would have expected to beat.

Anton Stach, already the provider of Pio Esposito's cup opener against Como days earlier, delivered the assist for Maximilian Beier to equalise in the 86th. The German striker has a habit of making decisive interventions even when the wider performance disappoints.
There was still time to nearly steal it. Pio Esposito struck a powerful shot in stoppage time, only for the Palermo goalkeeper to produce an outstanding save and keep the contest level.

The draw extends Napoli's league record to 12 wins, three draws and one defeat after sixteen matches. Beier now has 18 goals in all club competitions this season. But the result leaves plenty to analyse, not least how a team this talented can allow so many shots before halftime.

Peacock deserved better protection than he received. The two halftime arrivals were influential. And yet a second-half recovery was undone by another goal conceded on the break. The warning signs remain despite the resilience.

Napoli did not lose. There were moments when defeat seemed likely. Their final response avoided catastrophe, but a title contender cannot consistently require such rescues against the division's struggling sides.

Two points stayed in Palermo. The question now is whether Napoli can learn from a match in which their goalkeeper was too busy, their forwards were too often forced to rescue them, and a single point felt both precious and insufficient.

articles.label: SCUDETTO RACE · MATCHDAY 16
articles.imageCredit: Napoli title celebrations · archive illustration, not a photograph of a Roma fixture
articles.headline: ROMA BLINK. NAPOLI'S LEAD GROWS — DESPITE THAT PALERMO DRAW.
articles.dek: The champions were held 2–2 by bottom-club Palermo, but the verified standings show Napoli on 39 and Roma on 36 after 16 games each. A difficult afternoon somehow produces a wider advantage.
body: NAPLES — It was supposed to be the afternoon Napoli's wastefulness allowed Roma back into the title picture. The champions were held 2–2 away by Palermo. Instead, the confirmed Serie A table shows the lead over Roma has actually grown.
Napoli sit first on 39 points from sixteen matches. Roma have 36 from sixteen. Only two rounds earlier, the gap was two: Napoli had 35 points from fourteen, Roma 33.

Over those two rounds, Napoli beat Lazio 2–1 away and drew 2–2 at Palermo — four points from six. Roma's record changed from ten wins, three draws and one defeat to eleven wins, three draws and two defeats. That means one victory and one defeat, for a three-point return. The specific Roma opponents are not confirmed by the standings.

The difference is a single point gained by Napoli in the title race even after their own costly draw. The table now reads Napoli 39, Roma 36, Bergamo Calcio (Atalanta) 32, Juventus 31, Parma 26 and Milano FC (AC Milan) 25. Every side has played sixteen games.

The numbers are both comforting and revealing. Napoli have conceded just nine league goals through sixteen matches, the best defensive total among the leading six. Yet Peacock had to make six FIRST-HALF saves at Palermo before Beier rescued a late equaliser.

Roma have scored 35 goals and conceded 16, while Napoli have 31 for and nine against. The champions are three clear without playing like an irresistible attacking machine in their latest league outing.
The reasonable lesson is not that Napoli can afford to drift. It is that a league season sometimes gives you a chance to correct a problem without immediately being punished in the standings.

Juventus and Atalanta remain far enough behind to require a sequence of results, but neither is an irrelevance. Napoli have an upcoming home meeting with Juventus on January 27, after a demanding run that includes two Champions League away trips.
One can imagine the relief in Naples. The lead is real. So is the warning. Napoli cannot rely forever on other clubs dropping points in weeks when the champions themselves stumble.
For now, this is a remarkable piece of Scudetto arithmetic: one point at Palermo, but a larger cushion over Roma. The title race has offered Napoli a gift. Their next performances must justify it.

articles.label: GOALKEEPER DEBATE · PEACOCK'S EVIDENCE
articles.imageCredit: Napoli archival illustration; not presented as an image of Peacock's Palermo saves
articles.headline: PEACOCK MADE SIX SAVES IN 45 MINUTES. THE DEFENCE MUST GIVE HIM SOME HELP.
articles.dek: The young goalkeeper could not prevent two Palermo goals, but his first-half resistance kept Napoli within reach of a comeback. It is another noteworthy chapter in the club's goalkeeper discussion.
body: NAPLES — The scoreboard reads two goals conceded, but it does not tell the story of Peacock's afternoon. Six saves in the first half alone tell us more about how frequently Napoli exposed their goalkeeper against bottom-club Palermo.

Diakité put the hosts ahead in the 29th minute. A clean sheet was already impossible, and the opening half had become a survival exercise for a goalkeeper who expected a very different sort of assignment.

The second half shifted toward Napoli. Olise and Davies were introduced at halftime; McTominay equalised with an Olise assist, before Diakité scored a second on a counter. Beier's late intervention earned the visitors a point.

Nothing in the match report establishes Peacock as individually at fault for either Palermo goal. A goalkeeper can make several crucial stops and still be beaten. The quality of defensive protection matters.

Peacock has already earned attention for his contribution in the clean-sheet victory away at Monza, when he received Team of the Week recognition. This was another opportunity to show his value in demanding circumstances.

Alex Meret, meanwhile, produced a clean sheet at Borussia Dortmund in December, when Napoli's back line held the German side to just one save from its goalkeeper. Those are different tests of different defensive setups, not a simple argument for a permanent change.

Peacock's age and promise make his progress an important Napoli storyline. But individual heroics should not become the preferred way to assess him; six first-half saves against a struggling opponent are as much a criticism of the collective as a compliment to the goalkeeper.
The decision about future starts belongs to the football staff, and no public guarantee has been made. The evidence, however, keeps growing. Peacock is more than a name on a development chart.
Napoli can celebrate their young goalkeeper's resilience and still ask why he was required to demonstrate it quite so often.
The challenge in the next match is simple: a calmer afternoon for whoever wears the gloves.

articles.label: JANUARY 2029 · UPDATED TEN-MATCH SCHEDULE
articles.imageCredit: Pio Esposito in Napoli colours · archive player portrait illustrating January's fixture congestion
articles.headline: JANUARY’S GAUNTLET, UPDATED: TEN FIXTURES, TWO ROMA MATCHES AND JUVENTUS.
articles.dek: The updated January calendar now confirms ten matches, including the neutral January 1 Supercoppa final against Roma, shifted Parma/Palermo dates, and another cup match at Roma on January 31.
body: NAPLES — A schedule already regarded as demanding has become more intense. Napoli's updated January 2029 calendar now contains ten fixtures across three competitions' worth of commitments, including two different domestic cups, with Roma at either end of the month.

The first new appointment is the biggest: January 1, a Supercoppa Italiana final against Roma at a neutral venue. Roma qualified by beating Inter 3–2, while Napoli beat Milano FC 4–2 on penalties after a scoreless semifinal.
The final has no confirmed stadium or kickoff time. Its date is certain; its result is not. The match is the first of five scheduled games in the opening thirteen days.

Parma visit Naples on January 4 in Serie A, one day later than the January 3 date on an earlier calendar. Palermo now arrive January 7 rather than January 6. The league fixtures have shifted, not been played.
Fiorentina away on January 10 and Lazio at home on January 13 complete an opening sequence at three-day intervals: January 1, 4, 7, 10 and 13. Squad depth will be tested almost immediately.

Next come the European dates. Napoli visit Real Sociedad on January 16, then travel to KS Cracovia on January 24 for the final two listed Champions League league-phase matches. The last verified continental record is ten points after six matches.

Between those journeys, Napoli play Sampdoria away in Serie A on January 21. Juventus visit Naples on January 27, a fixture with obvious consequences given the clubs' position near the top of the league.

The new closing date is January 31, when Napoli are scheduled to travel to Roma in a domestic cup fixture. This is a separate cup match from the neutral Supercoppa final on New Year's Day. The January 31 cup round has not been specified.

The result is a confirmed count of ten games: six Serie A, two Champions League, one Supercoppa final, and one further domestic cup tie. All ten are future fixtures in the confirmed current match record.

The revised calendar leaves few opportunities for a sustained reset between matches. Napoli must consider recovery, rotations and the challenge of maintaining a strong league campaign while chasing honours in knockout competition.
One thing is settled: nobody needs to invent a more difficult January for Napoli. The dates, opponents and competitions on the updated calendar are demanding enough.

articles.label: COPPA ITALIA · NAPOLI 2–1 COMO · FULL TIME
articles.imageCredit: Alphonso Davies in Napoli colours · archive portrait, not a photograph of the 90th-minute winner
articles.headline: 90 MINUTES. ONE LAST PASS. PHONZIE SENDS NAPOLI THROUGH THE NIGHT.
articles.dek: Esposito's early opener is cancelled out by Braunöder within four minutes. After a frustrating stalemate, two Napoli substitutes — Nico Paz and Alphonso Davies — combine in the 90th for a stunning 2–1 home cup victory.
body: NAPLES, 13 DECEMBER 2028 — For ninety minutes, Napoli looked at a Coppa Italia tie that refused to follow the script. Then Nico Paz found Alphonso Davies, and the Maradona was given the finish it had been waiting for. Napoli 2–1 Como. A winner at the very edge of normal time. One of those goals that turns frustration into a night to remember.

The decisive moment arrived in the 90th minute. Paz supplied the pass, Davies applied the finish, and Stefan Saladino's side had a lead it had almost run out of time to find. Both players began the night outside the starting XI. Both had been introduced by the time Napoli needed one final attacking connection.

The result was dramatic, but the evening had started with an entirely different kind of promise. Napoli had rotated heavily after away victories over Borussia Dortmund and Lazio, and Anton Stach was among those entrusted with a starting role in midfield.

At 17 minutes, Stach supplied Pio Esposito for the opener. It was a moment of immediate reward for a reworked side. The young striker, fresh from his Champions League goal in Dortmund, continued to find ways to make himself decisive.
The lead lasted just four minutes. Braunöder equalised for Como in the 21st, and the match was level again before Napoli had much chance to settle into an advantage.

By halftime, the score remained 1–1. Napoli had been the more threatening team, but the scoreboard offered no consolation for their superiority. The challenge was no longer to start well; it was to find a finish before the chance disappeared.

The rotated eleven included Peacock in goal; Calafiori, Buongiorno, Geertruida and Kayode in defence; McTominay and Stach in midfield; Moore, De Bruyne and Olise behind Esposito. Buongiorno started alongside Geertruida, while Bastoni was among those rested. The reshuffle was substantial, but Napoli did not abandon their responsibility to win.

The visitors had already demonstrated that one good Napoli spell could be undone almost immediately. For a long time after the interval, the same uncomfortable scoreline held. The home side kept searching for a way through.

And then the late change in cast made all the difference. Paz, a creator who has provided so much for this attack, delivered the decisive ball. Davies, the electric runner who had started on the bench, was there to turn it into a winning goal. The exact substitution minutes mattered less than the moment both were ready for.
The winning finish was the 90th-minute answer to a long and increasingly anxious wait. Whatever else the night had lacked in efficiency, Napoli produced the one action that settled it.
Stach's first-half assist, Esposito's opener and the late Paz-Davies link deserve their place in the telling. So, too, does the refusal to let the earlier equaliser become the end of the story.

Napoli have won 2–1 at home against Como in the Coppa Italia. The precise round of the competition is not the story of this night. The final minute is. When the clock reached ninety, Napoli found one more goal — and the Maradona found its voice.

articles.label: SERIE A · LAZIO 1–2 NAPOLI · FULL TIME
articles.imageCredit: Maximilian Beier in Napoli colours · archive portrait, not a photograph from Lazio away
articles.headline: THE LOANEE BITES. BEIER ANSWERS TWICE. NAPOLI LEAVE ROME WITH THREE POINTS.
articles.dek: Hasa, a Napoli player on loan at Lazio, cancels out Beier's 16th-minute opener. But a Pio Esposito assist releases the German for the 66th-minute winner and moves the champions to 38 Serie A points.
body: ROME, 9 DECEMBER 2028 — Maximilian Beier has become the constant in a Napoli attack full of moving parts. In Rome, he scored twice, and both goals mattered. Napoli won 2–1 away at Lazio to move to 38 points after fifteen league matches.

Beier opened the scoring in the 16th minute after Nico Paz supplied the decisive pass. It was an early reward for a Napoli side looking to build on its 1–0 Champions League victory at Borussia Dortmund four days earlier.

Then came a particularly awkward equaliser. Hasa, a Napoli player spending the campaign on loan at Lazio, scored in the 26th minute to make it 1–1. A familiar footballer in an unfamiliar shirt had interrupted his parent club's evening.

Napoli continued to threaten before the break. Lazio managed only one shot on target in the first half, yet that was enough to leave the teams level. For the visiting staff, the halftime problem was clear on the scoreboard even as Napoli's attacking play offered encouragement.

The second half demanded composure. Napoli had recently allowed Udinese to leave with a 1–1 draw after taking the lead, and another early advantage in Rome had disappeared. A point might have been acceptable in isolation; it was not the result the champions wanted.

In the 66th minute, the combination that has powered so many Napoli attacks returned. Pio Esposito played the provider and Beier applied the finish. The German's second of the night put Napoli back ahead, this time for good.

Two assists from two different creators — Paz for the opener, Esposito for the winner — underlined the range of service Beier can exploit. His final touch may attract the biggest headlines, but the movement around him is part of the story.

Napoli had gone to Dortmund and ground out a narrow European win with a disciplined defensive performance. In Rome they found another way: a striker refusing to let a surrendered lead become a surrendered result.

The final 1–2 takes Napoli to twelve wins, two draws and one defeat from fifteen Serie A matches, with 38 points and a goal difference of plus 22. Roma had been two points behind after fourteen matches apiece; the latest gap must await Roma's own result.

For Hasa, the goal was an individual moment against the club that owns his registration. For Napoli, the response was what mattered most. Beier scored first, Beier scored last, and the champions went home with all three points.
Next came the domestic cup and a home meeting with Como. Serie A points had been secured. The next task was ensuring momentum survived a different kind of test.

articles.label: BELLANDI'S COLUMN · THE FIRST LEAD
articles.imageCredit: Napoli supporters and title-era archive image · used as an illustration, not a photograph of the Como match
articles.headline: BELLANDI: NAPOLI HAVE LEARNED HOW TO WIN LATE. WHY CAN'T THEY HOLD AN EARLY LEAD?
articles.dek: Udinese equalised, Hasa equalised, Braunöder equalised. Two dramatic victories have softened the consequences, but a recurring lapse is worth discussing before a title race becomes less forgiving.
body: NAPLES — There is a thrilling way to win football matches, and then there is a reliable way. Right now Napoli are providing too much of the former for anyone to be certain they have mastered the latter.

Against Como, Pio Esposito scored after 17 minutes. Four minutes later Braunöder equalised. The Coppa Italia tie became an increasingly tense wait until Alphonso Davies finished a Nico Paz pass in the 90th minute.

Against Lazio four days earlier, Maximilian Beier put Napoli in front after 16 minutes. By the 26th, Hasa — a Napoli loanee, of all people — had drawn the Romans level. Beier eventually scored the winner in the 66th.

Before that, Udinese had been allowed back into a match Napoli led from the eighth minute, with Garcia making it 1–1 from a 63rd-minute corner. The games were different. The recurring theme was not: the champions scored first and still found themselves starting over.

I am not claiming that the same player, system or lapse caused all three equalising goals. There is not enough evidence to make that accusation. A corner is not the same as open play. Nor does one Como goal automatically mean that the goalkeeper, or a rotated defender, is to blame.
But at a club chasing another Scudetto, patterns deserve scrutiny even when the final result looks beautiful in tomorrow's newspaper.

The counterargument is persuasive. Napoli did win in Rome. They did find a 90th-minute answer against Como. Beier and Pio continue to influence games, Nico Paz has produced assists across both matches, and Davies added a cup winner when the pressure was highest.

And what about the much-discussed technical staff? Stefan Saladino remains responsible for the decisions. His long-serving assistant, Sandro Vitale, is now a familiar name to supporters, too. There is no need to invent their private conversations to ask whether the defensive organisation after a goal can become steadier.
The most useful question is not 'who should be blamed?' It is 'what can be improved before the same situation happens in a match where there is no 90th-minute rescue?'

Good teams win late. Great teams also know how to make an early lead boring. Napoli have shown they possess the first quality. A demanding December will reveal how much progress they can make on the second.
For now, let the supporters celebrate Davies. Just do not confuse drama with a sustainable plan.

articles.label: CONTRACTS · GEERTRUIDA STAYS
articles.imageCredit: Napoli archive club photograph · illustrative image, not a photograph of Geertruida signing a new contract
articles.headline: GEERTRUIDA SIGNS ON: TWO MORE YEARS FOR NAPOLI'S VERSATILE DEFENDER.
articles.dek: The 28-year-old defender, rated 82, agrees a two-year extension and remains part of the depth Napoli will need across a crowded December.
body: NAPLES — Lutsharel Geertruida has agreed a two-year contract extension with Napoli, keeping the versatile defender in Stefan Saladino's squad for the seasons ahead.
The 28-year-old arrived at the negotiations with eighteen months remaining on his existing deal. The additional two years leave three years and six months on his agreement.

Geertruida's value to Napoli has never rested solely on being the first name placed on a team sheet. An experienced, flexible defender is an asset in a squad juggling league, European and cup commitments.

Napoli have invested considerable resources in the back line. Bastoni, Buongiorno, Cucurella, Calafiori and Kayode all have significant responsibilities. Another trusted option makes rotation less of a gamble when matches arrive only a few days apart.

The contract agreement followed a week of positive defensive signs: Napoli defeated Borussia Dortmund 1–0 away in the Champions League, with their starting back four holding the hosts to a single save from Alex Meret.
Geertruida then entered the starting XI at home to Como in the Coppa Italia. He partnered Buongiorno in the centre of defence as Saladino rotated players following wins against Dortmund and Lazio.
The cup match was anything but routine. Esposito scored early from a Stach assist, Como's Braunöder equalised, and Davies eventually delivered a dramatic 90th-minute winner from a Nico Paz pass.

For Geertruida, the importance of remaining at Napoli is practical as much as ceremonial. Minutes must be earned against established teammates, and a crowded fixture calendar can present opportunities that a thinner squad would struggle to manage.
An extension is not a guarantee of a starting shirt, nor does it establish a new hierarchy overnight. It is a decision to retain an experienced footballer who can contribute as the campaign advances.
Napoli's message is continuity. For a club chasing trophies on multiple fronts, that is often an underrated kind of ambition.

articles.label: THE MEN ON THE BENCH · SANDRO VITALE
articles.imageCredit: Napoli's 2027–28 title celebrations · archive club photograph, not a posed portrait of assistant manager Sandro Vitale
articles.headline: THE SECOND VOICE: MEET SANDRO VITALE, SALADINO'S MAN IN THE DUGOUT.
articles.dek: Not a new arrival, not a hired yes-man. Alessandro 'Sandro' Vitale has been beside Stefan Saladino since the beginning. Now the sharp-minded Neapolitan assistant is stepping into focus.
body: NAPLES — His name may be new to the headlines, but Alessandro 'Sandro' Vitale is no new arrival at Napoli. The assistant manager has occupied the seat beside Stefan Saladino since the beginning of the project. Across an unbeaten Scudetto campaign, a Coppa Italia triumph, a European final and the difficult months of a title defence, his place in the technical area has been constant.

For much of that time, Napoli's attention has rested where it usually does: on the manager, the players and the scoreline. And perhaps that is precisely the sort of arrangement Vitale prefers. There are coaches who thrive on cameras. Napoli's number two has built a different identity — serious about the details, sparing with grand gestures and quick with dry humour.

A Neapolitan by origin and an analyst by temperament, Vitale's interests range from how a midfield receives possession under pressure to the distances between defenders, the risks of pressing high and the cost of one poorly protected transition. It is the less glamorous part of the football conversation, right up until it decides a match.

His remit is broad: helping the manager assess opponents, examining what the team is doing well or badly, challenging a tactical assumption when the evidence warrants it and working through the uncomfortable questions that follow defeats. In a club as demanding as Napoli, agreeable advice has little value if it is also wrong.

'My job is to give the manager the clearest picture I can. He makes the decision. We live with the result together,' Vitale says. There is no attempt to borrow the authority of the man in charge — nor to disguise the responsibility of the staff around him.

That distinction matters. Saladino does not employ Vitale to nod on command; he employs him to offer a genuine second judgment. The manager can make a different call, and often must. The test of the relationship is not whether the two men agree every time, but whether their disagreements produce better decisions.

Their shared record already provides the stakes. Napoli's 2027–28 Scudetto came without a league defeat, accompanied by Coppa Italia success. The same side then fell painfully short against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. Winning and disappointment have each offered their own lessons.

This season has demanded more. European defeats to Arsenal and PSG sharpened scrutiny, while the Serie A title defence has become a fight with Roma. The touchline can feel exposed when the team is winning and strangely crowded when it is not.

Matteo Bellandi has previously directed public criticism toward Napoli's assistant-manager role. He is entitled to ask whether the work of the technical staff translates onto the grass. Vitale, equally, is entitled to let performances supply the argument rather than stage a public feud.

Wednesday's 1–0 victory in Dortmund was one of those performances. Pio Esposito scored from Maximilian Beier's pass, and a back four featuring Cucurella, Bastoni, Buongiorno and Calafiori restricted the hosts to a single save from Alex Meret. Kayode came on to help preserve the advantage. It was the kind of collective result any coaching staff will value.

Yet nobody outside the staff room needs to invent who proposed which adjustment to appreciate the achievement. The players did the work, Saladino made the decisions and the staff supported the plan. Football has more than one pair of eyes on the touchline, but it still has one manager.

So here is the name to remember beside Saladino: Sandro Vitale. A loyal Napoli man who will offer an opinion, defend it when the evidence supports it and revise it when the evidence changes. Not the protagonist of the story — but an integral part of the team trying to write the next chapter.

articles.byline: Napoli Season Room · European Football Bureau
articles.label: CHAMPIONS LEAGUE · BVB 0–1 NAPOLI
articles.imageCredit: Pio Esposito in Napoli colours · archive player artwork, not a photograph from Dortmund
articles.headline: PIO STRIKES. NAPOLI HOLD FIRM. A SILENCED DORTMUND AND THREE POINTS.
articles.dek: Esposito's 27th-minute finish from Beier's assist ends Napoli's European scoring drought. Cucurella, Bastoni, Buongiorno and Calafiori protect a 1–0 lead as the champions reach 10 points in the Champions League.
body: DORTMUND, 5 DECEMBER 2028 — A difficult European run demanded a change of outcome, and Napoli delivered it in Germany. Pio Esposito's 27th-minute goal proved enough to beat Borussia Dortmund 1–0, giving Stefan Saladino's side three precious Champions League points and a clean sheet to take home.

After successive 2–0 defeats to Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain, Napoli had arrived with seven points from five matches and more questions than answers. The result in Dortmund does not erase those nights. It does give the Italian champions a platform from which to respond.

Napoli opened with intent. João Neves helped force an early corner and the visitors showed they had not travelled merely to defend. The breakthrough followed in the 27th minute, when Maximilian Beier supplied Esposito for the finish that separated the teams.

The combination was reassuringly familiar. Beier and Esposito have shared goals and assists repeatedly this season, and the same understanding that has carried Napoli in Serie A now made the difference on a demanding European stage.
Beier had an opportunity to add to the score shortly before halftime, but Gregor Kobel saved his effort. Dortmund remained within a single goal, and a difficult second period lay ahead.

The defence, however, refused to offer the home side an easy route back. Napoli began with Cucurella, Alessandro Bastoni, Alessandro Buongiorno and Riccardo Calafiori across the back, a unit that deserved attention for how little was required of the goalkeeper behind them.

Alex Meret, restored to the starting side, finished with a clean sheet and exactly one save. He handled the action required of him, but the more revealing figure may be the lack of saves necessary. Napoli's outfield defenders made this a collective shutout rather than a tale of spectacular rescue work.

Michael Kayode was introduced as a substitute to help close out the victory. The timing of that change was less significant than the outcome: the lead survived, and Borussia Dortmund could not find an equaliser.

At the final whistle it was Dortmund 0–1 Napoli, the score unchanged from the interval. An away European win, built on an attacker's decisive touch and a back line's sustained protection, is often worth more than a lavish performance that fails to collect the points.
Napoli now have 10 points from six Champions League fixtures: three wins, one draw and two defeats, with nine goals scored and ten conceded. Progress remains work to be done, not a completed task.

Esposito's goal also ended the run of European blanks against Arsenal and PSG. Beier recorded another assist, Kobel had kept the score respectable, and Napoli finally found a way to make one finish count for everything.

Lazio await on 9 December in Serie A. The league title race is still tight, with Roma two points behind the champions after fourteen matches each. But first, Naples has a European result to savour. One goal. One save required. Three points.

articles.label: CONTRACT NEWS · CUCURELLA STAYS
articles.imageCredit: Napoli's 2027–28 title celebrations · archive club photograph, not an image from Cucurella's contract signing
articles.headline: CUCURELLA COMMITS: NAPOLI KEEP A KEY DEFENSIVE PIECE.
articles.dek: The 30-year-old full-back agrees to extend his stay by another two years, reinforcing Napoli's defensive options as the European schedule intensifies.
body: NAPLES — Marc Cucurella has agreed a two-year contract extension at Napoli, securing the experienced full-back's future as Stefan Saladino's side navigate another demanding campaign on two fronts.

At 30, Cucurella is no longer viewed as a prospect whose next five seasons can be assumed. He is something different and perhaps more immediately valuable: an established defender trusted to compete in matches where small positional errors can carry enormous consequences.
The extension adds another two years to the existing agreement, leaving three years and six months on the player's deal. It is an important piece of squad continuity for the Italian champions.

The announcement arrives in a week when Napoli have needed their defensive resources. Udinese left the Maradona with a 1–1 draw on 2 December, a game in which the visitors equalised from a second-half corner.

Three days later in Dortmund, Napoli's response came from the back as much as the front. Cucurella was part of the starting defensive four alongside Bastoni, Buongiorno and Calafiori. Napoli protected Pio Esposito's 27th-minute goal to win 1–0 in the Champions League.

Only one save was required from Alex Meret that night. No single defender can claim exclusive ownership of a team clean sheet, but the group offered exactly the kind of resistance that underpins success in knockout-calibre contests.

Cucurella's value goes beyond simply being available. The demands on a full-back in Napoli's structure are constant: receiving under pressure, choosing when to advance, recovering position and working in concert with the nearest centre-back.

The competition for minutes has not diminished. Michael Kayode came on against Dortmund to help secure the result, another reminder that Napoli can change personnel without entirely changing their defensive identity.

That depth will matter immediately. Lazio come next in Serie A on 9 December, followed by Como in domestic cup competition on 13 December and further league and Supercoppa commitments later in the month.

Longer contracts carry their own questions about how a player's physical profile changes with age. For now, however, Napoli have chosen continuity in a position that can become expensive and difficult to replace.

Supporters will see the extension for what it is: an assurance that one of the squad's senior defensive options remains part of Saladino's plans. The rest must be earned on the pitch, week after week.

articles.label: FULL TIME · NAPOLI 1–1 UDINESE · 2 DEC
articles.imageCredit: Maximilian Beier in Napoli colours · archive player portrait, not a photograph from the Udinese fixture
articles.headline: BEIER PUNISHES UDINESE. SAVA RESCUES THEM. GARCIA MAKES NAPOLI PAY.
articles.dek: An eighth-minute interception puts Napoli in command, but two João Neves passes are denied by Sava before Garcia strikes from a 63rd-minute corner. The champions settle for 1–1 and Roma close to two points.
body: NAPLES, 2 DECEMBER 2028 — Maximilian Beier needed eight minutes to find Udinese's weak spot. He intercepted a pass travelling between the visiting centre-backs, strode clear and finished without assistance. Napoli had the lead and an early invitation to make the evening comfortable.
But Udinese goalkeeper Sava made certain that Napoli's promising start never became a decisive advantage. Twice before the interval, he stood between the home side and a second goal.

In the 29th minute João Neves threaded a superb ball through the defence to Beier. The forward had timed his movement, only to find Sava in his way. Five minutes later, in the 34th, Neves found the same runner with another incisive pass. Again Sava produced the save.

Three moments told much of the opening period: Beier's ruthless anticipation for 1–0, and two beautifully constructed chances that should have given Napoli breathing room but instead left the score untouched.

Saladino's side took a 1–0 lead into half-time. The performance had been positive, particularly in the timing of Neves's passes and Beier's movement beyond the defensive line. Still, the game remained a single set piece away from a different story.
That moment arrived in the 63rd minute. Udinese won a corner and Garcia found the equaliser. From early command to a level scoreboard, Napoli had watched their advantage evaporate.

The goal will invite questions about defending dead-ball situations. The precise marking breakdown has not been established, and the presence of Peacock in goal is not, by itself, evidence of an individual error. Napoli must examine how the chance arose before assigning blame.

Expected goals finished 2.3 for Napoli and 1.4 for Udinese. The home side created more, but this was not an evening in which the visitors posed no threat. Those numbers describe a missed opportunity rather than a match Napoli were certain to win.

Peacock remained in goal after his clean sheet and Serie A Team of the Week selection against Monza. The Udinese match ended without another shutout. The debate over the goalkeeper position can continue on what happens on the pitch, rather than on imagined backstage conversations.

The points tell their own story. Napoli stand first on 35 from fourteen league matches, with eleven wins, two draws and one defeat. Roma are second on 33 from fourteen; the cushion at the top is now just two points.

Napoli travel to Borussia Dortmund on 5 December for a Champions League fixture carrying its own urgency. Back-to-back 2–0 defeats against Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain have left the Italian champions with seven points after five European games.

At the Maradona, however, the question was simpler. Beier got the goal, Neves made the chances, Sava made the saves and Garcia took advantage. Napoli did enough to lead. They did not do enough to win.

articles.label: BELLANDI'S VERDICT · THE TWO-POINT RACE
articles.imageCredit: Alessandro Bastoni in Napoli colours · archive player portrait, not an image from the Udinese game
articles.headline: BELLANDI: NAPOLI HAVE A STRIKER IN FORM — AND STILL LET UDINESE ESCAPE.
articles.dek: A forward can score and still leave the decisive chances behind. A goalkeeper can concede without being at fault. The more uncomfortable question is why the champions are making narrow leads so fragile.
body: There is a tempting story to write about Napoli's 1–1 draw with Udinese: a goalkeeper changed, a corner conceded, two points lost. It is neat. It is also too easy.

Let us start where the real football started. Maximilian Beier anticipated a disastrous square pass between Udinese's centre-backs and punished it after eight minutes. That was alert, confident forward play. The champions had been handed a beginning other teams would envy.

Then João Neves began to unlock the match. In the 29th and 34th minutes he sent Beier through with passes that should have made every Udinese defender question the space behind them. Sava answered on both occasions.

The instinct is to absolve Beier because he had already scored. I disagree. Great forwards do not stop being accountable after the first finish. He helped build the lead; he also had opportunities to extend it. Both truths can sit in the same column.
Equally, credit Sava. Two saves against well-timed runs are not a footnote. They are why Udinese were still within reach of a single set piece when the 63rd minute arrived.

Garcia then equalised from a corner. Napoli's set-piece defending deserves a serious review, though I will not pretend to know whether the lapse lay with a particular marker, a zone or the goalkeeper. You can criticise a collective outcome without inventing an individual culprit.

What concerns me is the pattern of risk. Napoli dominated the most memorable attacking sequences, but the final xG was 2.3 to 1.4. Udinese had opportunities of their own. Protecting a one-goal lead is a skill; avoiding the need to protect it is another.

The league does not wait for a champion to finish its tactical introspection. Roma now have 33 points from fourteen matches, Napoli 35 from fourteen. A two-point lead is an advantage, not a declaration of immunity.

Atalanta sit third on 28 and Juventus fourth on 25. It is Roma, however, who make every careless draw sting a little longer. A defending champion should not expect the chasing pack to forgive missed chances indefinitely.

There is good news in this irritation. Neves can see the passes. Beier can find the gaps. Napoli have the mechanisms to win matches without needing twenty shots and a miracle. Their problem on Saturday was making the work count.

And now Dortmund awaits. In Europe the champions have been blanked in consecutive 2–0 defeats. If Napoli want a more convincing argument about their continental ambitions, the response must come on the pitch, not in a promise.

No panic, then. But no applause for a draw merely because the expected-goals column looked flattering. The champions have higher standards than that — and the league table is beginning to insist upon them.

articles.label: PLAYER VOICES · BEIER ON NEVES, SAVA AND MISSED CHANCES
articles.imageCredit: Napoli's 2027–28 title celebrations · archive team photograph, not a photograph of this interview or Udinese match
articles.headline: BEIER: 'NEVES SEES THE RUN BEFORE I MAKE IT.'
articles.dek: Napoli's scorer reflects on an early interception, Sava's two saves and the uncomfortable feeling of leaving a winnable match level in a conversation with Giulia Romano.
body: After Napoli's 1–1 draw with Udinese, Maximilian Beier had a goal to his name and a result he could hardly celebrate. The German forward had scored after eight minutes, then watched Sava deny him twice before the break. Giulia Romano asked him about the moments that shaped the evening.
GIULIA ROMANO: That first goal came from an Udinese pass between the centre-backs. Did you sense the opportunity developing?

MAXIMILIAN BEIER: 'You try to stay awake when they're moving the ball across the back. Sometimes nothing happens. This time the pass was there, and I had to go. Once you're through, you're thinking only about finishing.'
ROMANO: Then João Neves finds you twice in the space of five minutes. What makes those passes so difficult to defend?
BEIER: 'João sees the run before I make it. That's the feeling. I look up and the ball is already coming into the space. As a striker that's what you want — you don't have to stop, turn and wait.'
ROMANO: Both chances ended with saves by Sava. How much frustration do you carry after a match like this?
BEIER: 'Some, of course. You can score early and still think about the ones you didn't score. Their keeper did his job very well. I have to look at what I could do better as well.'
ROMANO: Is it difficult to stay patient when you keep getting into good positions but the second goal won't arrive?
BEIER: 'You cannot let the last chance decide the next one. If João plays that pass again, I'm making the run again. That's football. You keep arriving and you try to be ready.'
ROMANO: Roma are two points behind Napoli. Does the table sharpen the disappointment?
BEIER: 'We know what the table looks like. You don't need someone to remind you. But we can't play every minute staring at another team's points. Today we wanted three. We got one.'
ROMANO: Dortmund next, and a return to Germany for you. How do you approach a European night after a draw like this?
BEIER: 'You take the lesson and then you go again. It's a different competition, a different match. We need to be sharp when our chances come. That's where my head is.'

Beier had taken his chance in the eighth minute, but Sava denied him in the 29th and 34th, and Garcia levelled in the 63rd. Now comes Dortmund, where another run beyond the defence could change an evening — provided the finish is there.

articles.label: THE GOALKEEPER DEBATE · TEAM OF THE WEEK
articles.imageCredit: Napoli's 2027–28 title celebrations · archive team photograph, not Peacock or the Monza match
articles.headline: PEACOCK'S BREAKAWAY SAVE LIGHTS UP MONZA — AND EARNS TEAM OF THE WEEK.
articles.dek: The young Napoli goalkeeper starts away to Monza, denies a one-on-one, keeps a clean sheet and earns a place in Serie A's Team of the Week. His first major spotlight belongs to what he did on the pitch.
body: MONZA, 26 NOVEMBER 2028 — Peacock's name is in Serie A's Team of the Week, and the reason is not difficult to find. Starting in Napoli's 3–0 away victory, the young goalkeeper faced a Monza breakaway and kept his goal intact. One sharp intervention, one clean sheet and a place among the standout performers of the round.

Most of Napoli’s attacking excitement belonged to Pio Esposito and Maximilian Beier. Beier scored in the 43rd and 53rd minutes, either side of Esposito’s 48th-minute goal. Each goal came from a pass by the other forward. Peacock's moment, however, arrived at the other end.

Monza broke through and found a route towards goal. The Napoli goalkeeper was exposed to a breakaway chance and made the save. A chance to dent the leaders’ advantage disappeared; the visitors went on to complete their shutout.
Peacock's reflexes were on display in the one-on-one. The clean sheet required contributions throughout the side, but that sharp save was a highlight all of its own.

After the final whistle came recognition: Peacock was selected in Serie A's Team of the Week. It is an accolade earned on the field rather than a prediction about how he might perform in the future. For a young keeper, the timing could hardly be better.

Napoli’s ninth league clean sheet is as much a team achievement as an individual one. After thirteen Serie A fixtures, the defending champions have conceded only five times. That protective structure helped turn an efficient attacking display at Monza into a comfortable 3–0 away victory.

Goalkeeping can be an unforgiving job. A forward can recover from a missed chance with another finish; a keeper may only get one big moment to influence the score. At Monza, when an opponent broke clear, Peacock was ready.

The next Napoli fixture is Udinese at home on 2 December. Borussia Dortmund follow away in the Champions League on 5 December. The crowded schedule will bring more decisions and more opportunities, with supporters eager to discover whether Peacock's latest performance earns him another appearance.

There is no need to manufacture a dispute to understand the significance of his week. The team sheet showed Peacock in goal, the scoreboard showed a clean sheet, and the league's weekly selection put his name in the spotlight.
An important save, three points, an award. Peacock left Monza with all three — and a moment to remember.

articles.label: FULL TIME · MONZA 0–3 NAPOLI · 26 NOV
articles.imageCredit: Maximilian Beier in Napoli colours · archived player portrait, not a photograph from the Monza match
articles.headline: PASS. FINISH. REPEAT. PIO AND BEIER DISMANTLE MONZA IN TEN MINUTES.
articles.dek: 43′ Beier from Pio. 48′ Pio from Beier. 53′ Beier from Pio. Three goals, three direct combinations, and a 3–0 away win that takes Napoli to 34 Serie A points.
body: The first half was nearly over when the two forwards began trading favours. In the 43rd minute Pio Esposito played Maximilian Beier, who finished to put Napoli in front away to Monza. At the interval, that was the game's only goal. The second half had barely begun before they went again.

At 48 minutes, Beier reversed the roles. This time he played Pio and the striker scored to double the lead. Five minutes later, in the 53rd, Esposito returned the pass in spirit and Beier scored again. MONZA 0–3 NAPOLI. The scoreboard had changed three times in ten minutes, and every goal had both players' fingerprints on it.

Three goals, three direct combinations. The scoring sequence was clear: 43′ Beier, assisted by Pio; 48′ Pio, assisted by Beier; 53′ Beier, assisted by Pio. Beier finished with two goals and an assist. Esposito finished with a goal and two assists.

The performance followed an even more extravagant partnership display against Atalanta, when Pio scored three and assisted three in a 6–2 victory and Beier produced two goals and two assists. If anyone wanted evidence that the front two are more than isolated goalscorers, the next league game supplied it almost immediately.

After Monza, Beier's 2028–29 Napoli club record across competitions stands at fourteen goals and six assists. Pio has eleven goals and ten assists. Their understanding is making the difference for the champions.

Monza had a chance to spoil the clean sheet. Peacock, in goal for Napoli, made a breakaway save. The young goalkeeper finished the 3–0 victory without conceding and was subsequently named to Serie A's Team of the Week.

The result lifted Napoli to eleven league wins, one draw and one defeat from thirteen fixtures. Thirty-four points, twenty-six goals scored, five conceded and a plus-twenty-one goal difference. It was the team's ninth Serie A clean sheet this season. Paris had stopped Napoli scoring in the Champions League; Monza could not contain the partnership.

The timing matters for the Scudetto race. Roma were unbeaten and just one point behind after twelve rounds, the last full standings snapshot available before Monza. Napoli have now moved to 34 points after thirteen. Roma's latest result must be factored in before anyone can pin down the current margin.

Three goals, all created and finished between the same two players, are enough to tell the story of this away victory. Napoli were clinical, the front pair irresistible, and the clean sheet completed a fine performance.

Udinese come to Napoli on 2 December, then Borussia Dortmund offer a European examination on 5 December. The unanswered question from recent continental defeats is whether this Napoli attack can find the same precision against the opposition that has been shutting it out. Against Monza, the answer was emphatically yes.

articles.label: SERIE A AWARDS WATCH · PIO ESPOSITO
articles.imageCredit: Pio Esposito in Napoli colours · archived player artwork, not a photograph from the Monza match
articles.headline: THE GOLDEN BOOT RACE AND THE ASSIST CROWN? PIO WANTS BOTH.
articles.dek: Another goal and two assists at Monza put Esposito tied for the Serie A scoring lead and out in front for assists. One forward, two leaderboards, and a title defence to carry.
body: There are strikers who live for goals. There are creators who measure their matches in final passes. Pio Esposito, in this Napoli side, has made a habit of refusing to choose. The Serie A leaderboards now place him joint top of the scoring race and alone at the top of the assists table.
Esposito shares first place among league scorers and holds outright first in assists. It is an extraordinary double presence at the top of Serie A’s individual leaderboards.

Monza supplied a neat illustration of how he has arrived there. At 43 minutes, he set up Beier. At 48, Beier played him in to score. At 53, Pio returned the favour with another assist for Beier. It was a goal and two assists in the same game, every Napoli goal directly involving the two attackers.

Those combinations built on an almost improbable 6–2 win over Atalanta. Pio had scored a hat trick, supplied three assists, and been involved in all six Napoli goals. Beier had struck twice and created two more. It was not just Pio's finishing that changed the scoreline; it was the way he made his partner better.

Across all 2028–29 club competitions, Pio has amassed eleven goals and ten assists — twenty-one direct goal contributions. Beier stands at fourteen and six — twenty. Their numbers are close, their movements intertwined, and their division of labour changes from chance to chance.

In 2027–28, Esposito scored twice in the Champions League final against PSG, including a 90th-minute equaliser that carried Napoli into extra time before Paris won 3–2. That heartbreak became a foundation for his growth into the attacking face of the defending Italian champions.

There is a useful caution in the praise. Napoli have not scored in their past two Champions League matches, losing 2–0 at Arsenal and 2–0 at home to PSG. Pio's Serie A brilliance does not by itself answer the questions those games raised. A great domestic campaign and a frustrating European spell can coexist.

The wider league race is equally unforgiving. Napoli hold 34 points from thirteen matches. Roma's previous table showed them unbeaten on 30 from twelve; the result of their next fixture will determine the latest gap. What is certain is that Pio's scoring and playmaking has become central to keeping Napoli in the Scudetto fight.

Individual honours cannot be awarded in November, and no trophy belongs to him yet. But being tied at the top of one major league chart while leading another is not normal striker business. It is the kind of double pursuit that can define a season if he sustains it.

When the next fixtures arrive — Udinese at home, then Dortmund away — the same question will follow Esposito from stadium to stadium: will he finish the move or create it? The frightening answer for opposing defenders is that they may have to prepare for both.

articles.label: WHAT COMES NEXT · UDINESE AND DORTMUND
articles.imageCredit: Alessandro Bastoni in Napoli colours · archived player portrait, not a photo from either future fixture
articles.headline: 34 POINTS, NINE SHUTOUTS — AND EUROPE IS STILL WAITING.
articles.dek: Napoli leave Monza with three goals, Peacock's Team of the Week recognition and a ninth league clean sheet. Now Udinese and Dortmund bring a demanding test of the champions' depth.
body: At the top of Serie A, Napoli's numbers are formidable: thirteen played, eleven wins, one draw, one loss, 34 points and only five goals conceded. Nine clean sheets already. The defending champions have the domestic record of a side that knows how to manage a long campaign.

Europe has been less forgiving. Napoli have conceded ten in five Champions League fixtures and failed to score in consecutive 2–0 defeats to Arsenal and Paris Saint-Germain. The contrast with their league performances is stark, even if those European opponents present different challenges.

Monza was the response the players could produce on the pitch. Beier scored twice, Pio Esposito added the other goal, and the pair assisted one another on each finish. Peacock made a crucial breakaway save, kept a clean sheet and earned Serie A Team of the Week honours.

The two forwards are now responsible for another remarkable set of combinations. Their quick passing and intelligent movement overwhelmed Monza in a ten-minute stretch spanning half-time. Napoli will want that attacking fluency when stronger European defences close down the space.

Udinese visit on 2 December in Serie A. Dortmund host Napoli in the Champions League on 5 December. There are just three days between those fixtures, and maintaining performance across both will be a test of the whole squad.

Peacock's Team of the Week appearance adds an encouraging option for Napoli, and his Monza stop was an eye-catching defensive highlight. Whether he appears against Udinese or Dortmund remains to be seen; the fixtures have yet to be played.

The league table is still demanding. Napoli have 34 points from thirteen matches. Roma were unbeaten on 30 from twelve in the last complete snapshot available, so the current point gap depends on their next result. Napoli cannot afford to assume the title defence will take care of itself.

December will bring further challenges: Lazio away on the 9th, Como in the cup on the 13th, Palermo and Bologna in the league, then AC Milan in the Supercoppa on the 29th. The schedule makes squad depth and consistency essential.

The key message from Monza is one of opportunity. A promising goalkeeper had his moment. The forwards rediscovered their ruthless link-up play. Napoli collected another three points and moved on to 34.

The next challenge is to take those qualities into tougher contests. A victory at Monza does not undo defeat to PSG, but it proves Napoli still have the attacking and defensive pieces to shape what happens next.

articles.headline: THE GHOST RETURNS. KVARATSKHELIA STRIKES AGAIN AS PSG SILENCE NAPOLI.
articles.dek: Ousmane Dembélé puts Paris ahead at 23 minutes against the run of early chances. Kvaratskhelia delivers the crushing 84th-minute blow. Five months after the Champions League final, Napoli have lost 0–2 to PSG — and Europe is becoming an increasingly painful problem.
body: NAPOLI 0–2 PARIS SAINT-GERMAIN, FULL TIME. The European final had ended with Kvaratskhelia scoring the decisive goal in Manchester. The rematch, in Naples on 21 November, ended with the former Napoli star on the scoresheet again. This time Paris did not even need extra time.

Napoli created promising early openings but could not find a way past the Paris defence and goalkeeper. At the other end, Ousmane Dembélé finished a PSG chance in the 23rd minute. The hosts had the opportunities to shape the game differently, yet it was Paris who converted first.

HALFTIME: NAPOLI 0–1 PSG. The home support had seen attacking passages that deserved a better outcome, but the scoreboard belonged to Paris. The match carried an uncomfortable echo of Napoli’s recent trip to Arsenal: good moments with the ball, no breakthrough, and a visiting or home opponent ready to punish the lapse.

Napoli had gone down 2–0 to Arsenal in their previous Champions League outing on 31 October. The prospect of another European blank became more uncomfortable as the PSG clock advanced. The travelling side’s second-half defensive organisation held up as Napoli searched for a route back.

In the 84th minute, the second blow arrived. KHVICHA KVARATSKHELIA — the man who struck at 54 and 110 minutes for PSG in last May's 3–2 extra-time Champions League final win over Napoli — scored again to make this rematch 0–2. The former Napoli icon now has three confirmed PSG goals against Saladino's side across those two encounters.

The final at Old Trafford had at least given Pio Esposito two goals and one last dramatic 90th-minute hope. On 21 November Napoli found no reply. Dembélé's 23rd-minute opener and Kvaratskhelia's 84th-minute goal were enough for PSG. Their finishing proved decisive, just as it had in May.

That result leaves Napoli's 2028–29 Champions League league-phase record at five matches, two wins, one draw and two defeats. Seven points; eight goals scored; ten conceded; goal difference minus two. Napoli have gone two consecutive European matches without scoring, after Arsenal 2–0 Napoli and Napoli 0–2 PSG.

The larger story extends beyond a single selection. Napoli have conceded ten goals in five European matches, a sharp contrast with their domestic defensive record. Those figures place the whole side’s organisation under the microscope: the spacing ahead of the back four, protection in transitions and the quality of opponents’ chances all demand scrutiny. No one isolated incident can explain the difference.

There was another layer to the reunion. João Neves, who equalised for PSG against Napoli in the 2028 final, now belongs to the Italian champions after his $250 million summer transfer. Whatever the tactical outcome of this November meeting, that reversal of shirts remains one of the competition’s most compelling subplots.

Napoli remain Serie A leaders with 31 points from twelve matches in the most recent completed round, one ahead of unbeaten Roma. Those league numbers are unchanged by defeat to Paris. The next game is away to Monza on 26 November; Borussia Dortmund await in the Champions League on 5 December.

The title race is alive, the European table remains recoverable and the season has not collapsed. But the central question cannot be avoided. Napoli scored six against Atalanta, then none against PSG. Saladino's side once came within ten minutes of penalties against these opponents. Five months later, the pain is still here — with another Kvaratskhelia goal stamped across it.

articles.label: EUROPEAN REVIEW · NAPOLI'S TWO SCORING BLANKS
articles.imageCredit: Alessandro Bastoni in Napoli colours · archived team portrait; no claim of goalkeeper or match action
articles.headline: EIGHT SCORED, TEN CONCEDED. WHAT HAS HAPPENED TO NAPOLI IN EUROPE?
articles.dek: After 2–0 defeats to Arsenal and PSG, Napoli's European figures stand in startling contrast with their Serie A dominance. The questions are tactical, collective and still unanswered.
body: Two Champions League evenings, two defeats by the same scoreline, and no Napoli goals. Arsenal won 2–0 on 31 October; Paris Saint-Germain followed with a 2–0 victory in Naples on 21 November. For a side capable of scoring six against Atalanta, the continental drought makes an unavoidable football story.

After five league-phase matches, Napoli have seven points: two wins, one draw and two defeats. They have scored eight goals and conceded ten. The attack that looks irresistible for long stretches of Serie A has been contained by two elite European opponents in succession.

Against PSG, Napoli fashioned the better early openings but failed to convert. Ousmane Dembélé gave Paris the lead after 23 minutes and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia made it 2–0 in the 84th. Across the tie’s decisive moments, PSG finished while Napoli failed to turn their threatening possession into goals.

Arsenal supplied a similar lesson, though the exact match patterns were not identical. A bright Napoli first half in London ended goalless before Arsenal scored twice after the break. The most useful question is not who to blame for a single miss but how Napoli can make their better periods count against opponents who give up fewer chances.

Conceding ten in five European matches is a team problem as well as a number. Napoli’s shape when moves break down, the space between midfield and defence, and the need to limit high-quality counterattacks are all elements worth examining. A clean defensive record in Serie A cannot simply be transplanted into a Champions League match.

The opposition matters too. Arsenal and PSG can defend deep phases, press on triggers and turn a transition into a goal without dominating every minute. Napoli's combinations still create openings, but European sides have been better at surviving those spells and striking back.

Pio Esposito and Maximilian Beier remain the creative core of Napoli’s domestic surge. Their partnership, so prolific against Atalanta, offers the clearest route back to goals. The challenge is to give both forwards the right service and space when top-level opponents deny them time between the lines.

The season is far from lost. Seven points after five European matches leaves games to play and adjustments to make. Napoli do not need an invented dressing-room crisis or a manufactured public quarrel to recognise that the last two results have been disappointing.

The next major European test comes against Borussia Dortmund away on 5 December. Before that, Napoli travel to Monza on 26 November and host Udinese on 2 December. Domestic fixtures offer a chance to rebuild sharpness, but the Champions League questions will not be resolved until another European whistle blows.

Two scoreless defeats deserve analysis, not scapegoats. The next Napoli side to take the field in Europe must prove it can defend dangerous moments and still deliver decisive attacking football. That balance, rather than one player’s reputation, is the real subject of this inquest.

articles.headline: MONZA NEXT. ROMA ONE POINT BACK. A SCUDETTO LEAD TO DEFEND.
articles.dek: The champions travel to Monza on 26 November as Serie A leaders on 31 points, with Roma unbeaten on 30. After European disappointment, domestic consistency comes first.
body: NAPOLI TRAVEL TO MONZA ON 26 NOVEMBER, and the brief is no longer simply to bounce back from a European defeat. It is also to protect the smallest possible advantage at the top of Serie A: one point.

The latest Serie A table after Napoli’s Atalanta victory contains twelve completed matches for each of its top six clubs. Napoli lead with 31 points, a 10–1–1 record and plus-eighteen goal difference. Roma have 30, nine wins, three draws, no defeats and an identical plus-eighteen goal difference. The Scudetto margin is thin.

Atalanta sit third on 24 after their 6–2 defeat to Napoli; Juventus and AC Milan are level on 22, and Lazio have 20. Those standings show the pressure on the league leaders: the next three points must be earned away from home.

Napoli's domestic attack is anything but short of evidence. Pio Esposito has ten goals and eight assists across club competitions, Beier twelve and five. They combined for five goals and five assists between them against Atalanta, sharing one another's finishing and creating. Nico Paz scored the sixth. In Serie A the front line has been formidable.

The PSG defeat adds urgency. Napoli have failed to score in their last two Champions League games, both 2–0 losses. Serie A has produced far better attacking returns, and Monza is the immediate chance to restore momentum without forgetting the challenges that await in Europe.

There is also the familiar anticipation of a new team sheet. Napoli have options throughout the squad and an increasingly demanding December programme. Selection and rotation could shape the next stretch, but no early line-up prediction should overshadow the trip itself.

Against Monza, Napoli’s ability to move the ball quickly through midfield and find Pio and Beier between defenders is likely to matter more than headlines. The visitors need to build pressure without leaving the counterattack exposed.

Monza should not be written off. Away fixtures carry their own complications, particularly when the visitors arrive after two difficult European nights. Napoli cannot count on reputation or recent home performances to deliver three points.

A victory would lift Napoli to 34 points. The precise gap at the top afterward will depend on Roma's next outing. Six days after Monza, Udinese come to Naples on 2 December. Three days later, Dortmund provide the next major Champions League examination away.

Monza is the immediate business. The champions need points, and the Pio–Beier partnership has the talent to provide them. A positive result would give Napoli a stronger platform before Udinese and Borussia Dortmund arrive on the fixture list.

articles.label: 21 NOVEMBER · CHAMPIONS LEAGUE · PSG AT NAPOLI
